calculus.title: Watch a teacher choose the method
calculus.summary: Four comparisons: average against instantaneous, product rule against expanding, naming the inside, and area against antiderivative.
calculus.intro: Four worked comparisons where more than one route is available. In each one I pick a method, say why, then run the alternative and check that the two agree. The point is the choosing, not the answer.
calculus.needs: Use after the derivative units. Every calculation is carried out in full, and each chapter ends by saying when the other route would have been easier.

parts.title: Average rate or instantaneous rate?
parts.goal: Tell apart the two questions, and see why they sometimes give the same number.
opening: Position follows s(t) = t² metres. Someone asks for “the velocity” between t = 1 and t = 3. That phrasing hides two different questions, and they need different tools.
I will answer both, then show why they happen to agree here — and construct a case where they do not, so the agreement is not mistaken for a rule.

steps.title: Separate the two questions
steps.line: Average over 1 ≤ t ≤ 3, or the velocity at one instant?
steps.why: An average needs two observations and an interval. An instantaneous velocity needs a derivative at a single point. Deciding which is being asked is the whole first step.

steps.title: Compute the average
steps.why: Change in output over change in input, using the same two observations for both. This is one number standing in for the whole interval.

steps.title: Compute the instant
steps.why: The derivative is what the interval averages settle toward as the interval closes around t = 2. Same number as the average — which deserves an explanation rather than a shrug.

steps.title: Explain the agreement, then break it
steps.line: For s = t² the average over [a,b] is a+b, and s′((a+b)/2) = a+b. For s = t³ over [1,3]: average 13, but s′(2) = 12.
steps.why: For a quadratic the average over an interval always equals the derivative at the midpoint. That is a property of quadratics, not a general law, and the cubic shows it failing.

parts.ending: The two questions coincide for quadratics at the midpoint and diverge otherwise. Decide which one was asked before reaching for a method.

parts.title: Product rule, or expand first?
parts.goal: Run both routes on the same expression and find where only one of them is available.
opening: For y = x²(x + 3) there are two honest routes: multiply the brackets out and differentiate term by term, or apply the product rule directly.
Both are correct. I will run them side by side, then find the case where the easier one is simply not on offer.

steps.title: Expand first, because it needs no new rule
steps.why: When a product multiplies out in one line, this is usually the fastest and least error-prone route. The power rule alone does the work.

steps.title: Now the product rule
steps.why: Each factor's rate is multiplied by the other factor's full size. Getting the same answer is the check that the rule was applied correctly.

steps.title: Find where expanding stops working
steps.why: With an unspecified second factor there is nothing to multiply out, so the product rule is the only route. This is the case the rule exists for.

steps.title: State the choice
steps.line: Expand when the product is short and multiplies out; use the rule otherwise.
steps.why: Neither is more correct. The rule is more general, expanding is often quicker, and running both is a free check when the expression allows it.

parts.ending: Two routes, one answer. Expanding is a shortcut that exists only sometimes; the product rule always works and doubles as the verification.

parts.title: Name the inside before differentiating
parts.goal: Apply the chain rule to a composite and catch the most common dropped factor.
opening: For y = (3x + 2)² the tempting answer is 2(3x + 2). It is wrong, and the reason is a factor that is easy to lose because it never appears on the page.
I will name the inside explicitly, differentiate each layer, then check the result by expanding — which is exactly the check that exposes the missing factor.

steps.title: Give the inside a name
steps.why: Writing the substitution down turns one composite expression into two simple ones, each with its own obvious derivative.

steps.title: Differentiate each layer separately
steps.why: Two rates answering different questions: output per unit of the inside, and inside per unit of x.

steps.title: Multiply the two rates
steps.why: The chain rule multiplies them because the units of the middle quantity cancel. The factor of 3 is precisely what the tempting answer omitted.

steps.title: Check by expanding
steps.why: The expansion agrees with the chain rule and disagrees with 2(3x+2) = 6x + 4. Whenever the composite can be expanded, this check settles the matter in one line.

parts.ending: The inside's rate is a factor, not an optional extra. Expanding is the cheapest way to catch it when the expression allows expansion.

parts.title: Area or antiderivative?
parts.goal: Get the same displacement two ways, then find where only one route survives.
opening: Velocity is v(t) = 2t m/s and we want the displacement from t = 1 to t = 3 seconds. The region under the line is a trapezoid, so geometry is available — and so is an antiderivative.
I will do both, use one to check the other, and then change the velocity rule so that geometry runs out.

steps.title: Read it off the graph
steps.why: A trapezoid's area is the average of the parallel sides times the width. For a straight-line velocity this is exact, not an approximation.

steps.title: Now use an antiderivative
steps.why: Both endpoint values are needed. Evaluating only at the top would give 9, which is an accumulation from nowhere rather than between the bounds.

steps.title: Show the constant cannot matter
steps.why: The constant appears in both endpoint values and cancels in the subtraction. That is exactly why a definite integral needs no +C.

steps.title: Change the rule so geometry fails
steps.line: v(t) = 3t² from 0 to 2: no simple area formula, but [t³]₀² = 8 − 0 = 8 m
steps.why: The region under a curve has no elementary area formula. The antiderivative route is unaffected, which is what makes it the general method.

parts.ending: Geometry and antiderivatives must agree wherever both apply. Geometry runs out as soon as the velocity graph stops being straight; the antiderivative does not.

physics.title: Watch a teacher pick the law
physics.summary: Four decisions: force or energy, which quantity a collision conserves, reading one graph three ways, and tracing a circuit before calculating.
physics.intro: Four problems where the hard part is choosing which law to apply. In each one I state the choice and the reason, work it through, then run the alternative to confirm that the physics agrees with itself.
physics.needs: Use after the force, energy, collision and circuit units. g = 10 m/s² and friction is ignored unless stated.

parts.title: Force or energy?
parts.goal: Choose between kinematics and an energy account, then confirm they agree.
opening: A 2 kg cart starts from rest on a frictionless track. A steady 10 N force pushes it through 3 metres. How fast is it moving at the end?
The question gives a force and a distance and asks for a speed. Both routes will work here; I will run each and then say which question would have made the choice matter.

steps.title: Notice what the question supplies
steps.line: Force 10 N, distance 3 m, mass 2 kg, starts from rest. No time is given or asked for.
steps.why: Force times distance is work, which is an energy quantity. When time appears nowhere in the question, the energy route usually goes straight to the answer.

steps.title: Energy route
steps.why: All the work done goes into kinetic energy because the track is frictionless and level. One equation, no intermediate quantities.

steps.title: Force route, for comparison
steps.why: The same answer by a different road. Agreement between two independent methods is the strongest check available in a physics problem.

steps.title: Say when the choice matters
steps.line: “How long did it take?” → t = v/a = 5.48/5 = 1.10 s
steps.why: The energy route never mentions time, so it cannot answer that. Choose the method by which quantities the question names and which it asks for.

parts.ending: Energy skips time and goes straight from force and distance to speed. Kinematics keeps time available. Both agree at 5.48 m/s.

parts.title: Which quantity does a collision conserve?
parts.goal: Use momentum for a sticking collision, and see what conserving the wrong quantity produces.
opening: A 2 kg cart moving right at 3 m/s strikes a stationary 1 kg cart and they stick together. External impulse during the brief contact is negligible.
Momentum and kinetic energy are both tempting. Only one is conserved here, and running the other one deliberately shows why it cannot be.

steps.title: Choose the conserved quantity
steps.line: Momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy is not.
steps.why: A sticking collision deforms the carts and makes sound, both of which remove kinetic energy. Nothing removes momentum from the pair, because the external horizontal impulse is negligible.

steps.title: Apply momentum
steps.why: Add mass times signed velocity for each object before impact; afterwards the combined 3 kg shares one velocity.

steps.title: Account for the energy
steps.line:
Before: ½(2)(3²) = 9 J
After: ½(3)(2²) = 6 J
Missing: 3 J
steps.why: The 3 J went into deformation and sound. Noticing where it went is what distinguishes a conserved quantity from one that merely changes form.

steps.title: Try conserving the wrong one
steps.line:
½(3)v² = 9 → v = 2.45 m/s
That carries 3 × 2.45 = 7.35 kg·m/s
steps.why: Momentum would have appeared out of nowhere, rising from 6 to 7.35 with no external push. The contradiction is the proof that kinetic energy is the wrong thing to conserve here.

parts.ending: Momentum gives 2 m/s and accounts for the missing 3 J. Conserving kinetic energy instead would manufacture momentum from nothing.

parts.title: One graph, three questions
parts.goal: Take height, slope and area from the same velocity–time graph without confusing them.
opening: A cart rises uniformly from 0 to 4 m/s over 0–2 s, holds 4 m/s from 2–4 s, then falls uniformly to rest over 4–6 s.
Three different questions can be answered from this one picture, and each uses a different feature of it. I will take them in turn and then name the trap.

steps.title: Decide which feature each question needs
steps.line: Velocity → height. Acceleration → slope. Displacement → area.
steps.why: Choosing the feature before calculating is what prevents reading a height where a slope was wanted. Most errors on these graphs are feature errors, not arithmetic ones.

steps.title: Acceleration from the slopes
steps.why: A flat segment has zero slope and therefore zero acceleration, even though the cart is moving fastest there. Height and slope are independent.

steps.title: Displacement from the areas
steps.why: Triangle, rectangle, triangle. Every segment is above the axis, so all three contributions are positive and the distance equals the displacement.

steps.title: Name the trap
steps.line: The falling line from 4–6 s still means forward motion.
steps.why: The graph is not a picture of the path. While the height stays positive the cart keeps moving forward; the fall only means it is doing so more slowly.

parts.ending: Height 0–4 m/s, slopes +2, 0 and −2 m/s², total displacement 16 m — three answers from one picture, each using a different feature.

parts.title: Trace the circuit before calculating
parts.goal: Work the same two resistors in series and in parallel, and sanity-check the direction of the answer.
opening: An ideal 6 V source drives a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor. The resistance labels alone do not determine the answer — the wiring does.
I will do both arrangements and finish with a check that catches the single most common error in this topic.

steps.title: Trace the path first
steps.line: One continuous loop → series. Two separate branches across the source → parallel.
steps.why: In series the same current passes through both; in parallel each resistor sees the full source voltage. Which quantity is shared is decided by the wiring, not the labels.

steps.title: Series
steps.line:
R = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω; I = 6/6 = 1 A
Drops: 1×2 = 2 V and 1×4 = 4 V, adding to 6 V
steps.why: One path, one current. The drops must add back to the source voltage, which is the check that the series calculation is right.

steps.title: Parallel
steps.why: Each branch independently sees 6 V, so compute the branch currents and add them. The equivalent resistance follows from the total current, not from adding the resistances.

steps.title: Check the direction of the result
steps.why: Opening a second path must make the pair easier for current than either resistor alone. Any parallel answer above the smallest individual resistance is wrong, and this check catches it immediately.

parts.ending: Series: 6 Ω and 1 A. Parallel: 1.33 Ω and 4.5 A. Trace the wiring first, then check that adding a path lowered the resistance.

medicine.subject: medicine
medicine.title: How the body keeps itself in range
medicine.intro: Eleven units on the mechanisms behind physiology and clinical reasoning: feedback, transport, pressure and flow, gas exchange, filtering, defence, drug levels and what a test result is actually telling you.

stages.title: The body as a regulated system
stages.goal: Set points, gradients, and why a single reading is not a story.

stages.title: Moving things around the body
stages.goal: Pressure, flow, gas exchange and the kidney's filter-then-reclaim design.

stages.title: Defence, drugs and evidence
stages.goal: Control loops that fail, immunity, drug levels and reading a test result.

units.title: Staying in range is active work
units.goal: Describe a negative feedback loop as sensor, comparator and effector, and say what the set point is.
opening: Core body temperature sits near 37 °C. It does not stay there because nothing disturbs it — a cold room, a fever, a hard run and a heavy meal all push on it continuously. It stays there because something measures it and pushes back.

That pushing back has a shape worth learning once, because the same shape turns up in blood glucose, blood pressure, salt, water and pH. A sensor reads the value, a comparator holds a target, and an effector acts in the direction that reduces the gap.
units.heading: Why the loop has to act in the opposite direction
teaching: Call the measured value the output and the target the set point. Negative feedback means the response has the opposite sign to the error: too hot triggers cooling, too cold triggers heating. If the response had the same sign as the error, every small disturbance would grow instead of shrink.

Control does not mean the value never moves. It means deviations are detected and corrected, so the value oscillates in a narrow band around the set point rather than drifting away. The narrowness of that band is what we are describing when we call something tightly regulated.
terms: The target value a control loop defends.
A response in the opposite direction to the error, which shrinks the gap.
The structure that carries out the correcting action — a sweat gland, a muscle, a hormone-secreting cell.

first.title: Cooling down after the temperature rises
first.problem: Core temperature rises from 37.0 °C to 37.5 °C during exercise. Trace the loop that brings it back.
steps: Receptors in the hypothalamus and in the skin report temperature. The hypothalamus is where the reading is compared with a target.
The sign matters more than the size here. A positive error means the body is above its target.
Error positive → act to lower temperature
Sweating and widening of skin vessels both move heat out. Both are responses with the opposite sign to the error.
Heat loss rises → temperature falls → error shrinks → response eases
As the error approaches zero the correcting action is dialled back. That self-limiting property is what makes the loop settle rather than overshoot indefinitely.
first.notice: Nothing in the loop needs to know why the temperature rose. The same machinery handles exercise, a hot room, and a heavy meal.

second.title: The same loop running the other way
second.problem: Core temperature falls to 36.5 °C in a cold room. What changes, and what stays the same?
steps: The error is now negative. The sensor and comparator are unchanged.
Error negative → act to raise temperature
Shivering generates heat; skin vessels narrow to keep it in. Different effectors, same rule.
Sweating and shivering are two outputs of one controller
The loop is not two separate systems. It is one comparator that can drive responses in either direction.
second.notice: A controller that can only push one way cannot hold a value in a band — it can only stop it going one direction.

exercise: Blood glucose rises after a meal and returns to its usual range over the next two hours. Name the error, the direction of the response, and one effector.

The error is positive: glucose is above its set point. The response must lower it, so insulin is released and tissues take glucose out of the blood. Insulin-secreting beta cells are the effector. The shape is identical to the temperature loop.

mistake.attempt: A fever means the body's temperature control has broken down.
mistake.diagnosis: During a fever the loop is working normally — it is defending a higher set point. The giveaway is the direction of the response: a person whose fever is rising feels cold and shivers, which is the body actively generating heat to reach the new target.
mistake.repair: Describe fever as a regulated change in the set point rather than a loss of regulation. The controller is intact; the target has moved.
mistake.check: Watch which way the effectors are pushing. A broken controller would not produce purposeful heat generation; it would simply let temperature drift with the room.

units.takeaway: A regulated value is held by a loop: sensor, comparator with a set point, and an effector acting in the opposite direction to the error. Regulation means deviations get corrected, not that the value never moves.

recall.ask: If a loop responded in the same direction as the error instead of the opposite one, what would happen to a small disturbance?
recall.answer: It would grow. A small rise would trigger a response that raised the value further, which would enlarge the error and trigger more of the same. That is positive feedback, which drives a value away from its starting point rather than holding it.

units.title: Why anything crosses a membrane at all
units.goal: Predict the direction of diffusion and osmosis from gradients, and say when a pump is required.
opening: A cell membrane is not a wall. It is a barrier that lets some things through easily, some things through slowly, and some things only with help and an energy supply.

Almost all of the movement you need to account for comes from one idea: substances spread from where they are concentrated to where they are not, until the difference is gone. Anything moving the other way needs a reason, and that reason costs energy.
units.heading: Name the substance before you name the direction
teaching: Diffusion moves a substance down its own gradient. Oxygen crosses from alveolar gas into blood because the partial pressure of oxygen is higher in the gas; carbon dioxide crosses the other way for the same reason, in its own gradient.

Osmosis is the special case of water. Water moves down the water gradient, which is toward the side with more dissolved solute, because that is the side where water itself is more dilute. Active transport moves a substance against its gradient and must be paid for with ATP, which is why the sodium–potassium pump is one of the body's largest standing energy costs.
terms: A difference in concentration or pressure between two places.
Movement of water across a membrane toward the higher solute concentration.
Movement against a gradient, powered by ATP.

first.title: Oxygen entering the blood
first.problem: Alveolar oxygen is about 100 mmHg; oxygen in the blood arriving at the alveolus is about 40 mmHg. Which way does oxygen move, and what stops it?
steps: 100 mmHg in gas vs 40 mmHg in blood
Partial pressure is the gradient that matters for a gas, not the total number of molecules.
Oxygen moves down its own gradient. No pump is involved, and none is needed.
Movement slows as the two pressures converge
Blood leaving a healthy alveolus is close to 100 mmHg. The gradient has mostly been used up.
CO₂: about 45 mmHg in blood, 40 mmHg in gas → blood to gas
Each gas follows its own gradient. They cross in opposite directions across the same membrane at the same time.
first.notice: A membrane does not decide direction. The gradient does, and each substance has its own.

second.title: A red cell placed in pure water
second.problem: A red blood cell is put into pure water. Which way does water move, and what happens to the cell?
steps: Inside: dissolved salts and proteins. Outside: none.
The inside has more solute, so the inside has proportionally less water.
Water moves inward, toward the higher solute
This is the same rule as diffusion, applied to water as the substance that is moving.
The cell swells and may burst
Nothing is pumping the water in. The gradient alone is enough.
second.notice: In 0.9 % saline there is no net water movement, because the solute concentrations are close to matched. That is why it is the default fluid for giving into a vein.

exercise: Sodium is far more concentrated outside a cell than inside, yet cells keep pushing sodium out. What does that tell you about the process, and what does it cost?

Moving sodium out is moving it against its gradient, so it cannot be diffusion. It is active transport, carried out by the sodium–potassium pump and paid for with ATP. Maintaining that gradient is one of the largest ongoing energy costs in the body.

mistake.attempt: Osmosis is strange because water moves from low concentration to high concentration — the opposite of diffusion.
mistake.diagnosis: Two different concentrations have been mixed up in one sentence. Water moves down the gradient of *water*, from where water is more concentrated to where it is less. That is exactly the same direction as any other diffusion; it only looks reversed when you track the solute instead of the water.
mistake.repair: Say which substance is moving. Water moves toward the higher *solute* concentration precisely because that is where water itself is more dilute.
mistake.check: Put 0.9 % saline on one side of a membrane and pure water on the other. Water moves toward the saline. Describe that as water moving down the water gradient and it obeys the ordinary rule with no exception needed.

units.takeaway: Name the substance, then find its gradient. Diffusion runs down a gradient for free; movement against a gradient is active transport and costs ATP. Osmosis is just diffusion with water as the substance you are tracking.

recall.ask: Blood sodium concentration is held in a narrow band. Name the error, the direction of the correction, and one effector.
recall.answer: If sodium concentration rises above the set point the error is positive, so the correction must lower it — by retaining water and by triggering thirst. Antidiuretic hormone acting on the kidney is one effector. Same loop shape as temperature.

units.title: Read a measurement as a story, not a score
units.goal: Interpret a vital sign using the person's baseline, the trend and the context rather than a population range alone.
opening: A heart rate of 110 is a number. On its own it does not say whether anything is wrong, because the same number arises in a frightened person, a person who just climbed stairs, a person with a fever, and a person losing blood.

What turns a number into information is three further things: what this person's own value usually is, which way it is moving, and what else is true at the same moment. This unit is about that reasoning, not about diagnosing anyone.
units.heading: A reference range describes a population, not a person
teaching: Published ranges such as 60–100 beats per minute are built to contain most healthy people. They are a starting assumption, not a verdict. A trained endurance athlete commonly sits in the 40s or 50s while entirely well, and a person whose usual rate is 85 may be unwell at 100 even though 100 is inside the range.

Readings also move together, because they are outputs of linked systems. A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure tells a different story from a rising heart rate with a normal blood pressure, because the first pattern suggests the body is working to compensate for something. Reading them one at a time discards that information.
terms: The value that is usual for this particular person.
The direction and speed of change across repeated readings.
A change in one variable that holds another one steady.

first.title: The same heart rate, two different stories
first.problem: Two people both have a heart rate of 110. One has a blood pressure of 125/80; the other has 85/50. What does the pairing add?
steps: The pressure is being held up. A fast rate with a normal pressure is consistent with fright, exertion, pain or fever — the circulation is not failing to deliver.
Here the fast rate has not succeeded in holding the pressure. The combination suggests the heart is speeding up to compensate for something and not fully succeeding.
Say what the single number was missing
The information lives in the relationship between the readings, not in either one.
A rate climbing 80 → 95 → 110 differs from one steady at 110 for a year
Direction over time carries as much weight as the current value.
first.notice: This is reasoning about measurement. Deciding what to do about any real person is a clinical judgement this course does not make.

second.title: A reading inside the range that is still a change
second.problem: Someone whose blood pressure is usually around 170/95 is measured at 120/80. The reading is squarely in the normal range. Is it unremarkable?
steps: 120/80 sits in the middle of the usual range
Judged against the population alone, nothing stands out.
A fall of about 50 mmHg systolic
Against their own history this is a large change, and large changes are what carry information.
Interpret against baseline first, population second
The population range answers 'is this value common?'. The baseline answers 'has something changed in this person?'
second.notice: A value can be normal for the population and abnormal for the person. Both comparisons are useful; neither replaces the other.

exercise: A person's respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, just above a typical adult range of 12–20. What three things would you want before treating that number as meaningful?

Their usual rate, the direction it has been moving, and what else is happening — temperature, oxygen saturation, whether they are in pain or anxious, and whether they have just moved. A single borderline value with no baseline, no trend and no context is close to uninformative.

mistake.attempt: A heart rate of 55 is below the normal range of 60–100, so it is abnormal and concerning.
mistake.diagnosis: A reference range describes most of a population; it does not describe this person. A trained athlete at 55 with a normal blood pressure and no symptoms is at their own baseline, whereas 55 in someone whose usual rate is 85 and who feels faint is a large change in the wrong direction. The same number carries opposite weight in the two cases.
mistake.repair: Read the number together with the person's baseline, the trend across readings, and the rest of the picture.
mistake.check: Ask what would change your mind. If the answer is 'nothing, 55 is simply out of range', the reasoning is using the population range as a verdict rather than as a prior.

units.takeaway: A vital sign becomes information when you add three things: this person's baseline, the trend, and what else is true at the same time. Readings also move together, so pairs carry more than singles.

recall.ask: Why does giving 0.9 % saline into a vein not make red cells swell or shrink?
recall.answer: Its solute concentration is close to that inside the cells, so there is no meaningful water gradient across the membrane and no net osmosis. Pure water would create a large inward gradient and make the cells swell.

units.title: Two circuits, one pump
units.goal: Explain why the two sides of the heart move equal volumes against very different pressures.
opening: Blood leaving the left side of the heart travels to the body and returns to the right side. Blood leaving the right side travels to the lungs and returns to the left. The two circuits are joined end to end, and the heart drives both from one housing.
That arrangement has a consequence worth stating plainly: because the circuits are in series, whatever volume one side moves, the other side must move too.
units.heading: Thickness reports pressure, not volume
teaching: The left ventricle wall is several times thicker than the right. The reason is the pressure each has to generate: roughly 120 mmHg systolic into the systemic circulation on the left, against roughly 25 mmHg into the pulmonary circulation on the right. The lungs are a low-resistance, low-pressure bed sitting right next to the heart.

Volume is a different question, and it is settled by the plumbing rather than by the muscle. Two pumps in series must move the same average volume per minute, or blood would accumulate on one side. Over a day, with an output near 5 litres a minute, that is roughly 7,000 litres through each side.
terms: Volume of blood leaving a ventricle per minute, about 5 L/min at rest.

first.title: Follow one red cell all the way round
first.problem: Trace a red cell from a leg vein back to the same leg vein, naming every chamber and vessel it passes.
steps: Leg vein → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle
This blood is oxygen-poor and carbon-dioxide-rich. It has already delivered its oxygen.
Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → alveolar capillaries → pulmonary vein → left atrium
Note the naming: the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood. Arteries are defined by leaving the heart, not by what they carry.
Left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → leg artery
Now the blood is oxygen-rich. One full circuit has crossed the heart twice.
Two passes through the heart per lap
That is what 'two circuits in series' means in practice.
first.notice: A red cell cannot travel from the body to the body without going through the lungs. The design forces every unit of blood past the gas exchanger.

second.title: Why the walls differ
second.problem: The left ventricle wall is about 10 mm thick, the right about 3 mm. Does the left side therefore pump more blood?
steps: State what the two sides must share
They are in series. Sustained inequality would pile blood up on one side within minutes.
The left ventricle generates roughly five times the pressure, and wall thickness tracks that requirement.
Both sides move about 5 L/min. Only one of them has to push it around the whole body.
second.notice: Pulmonary vessels are short, wide and low-resistance, which is why so much less pressure is needed to drive the same flow through them.

exercise: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood — the reverse of the usual pattern. Why are they still named artery and vein?

Because the names describe direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content. An artery carries blood away from the heart and a vein carries it back. In the pulmonary circuit that happens to put the oxygen-poor blood in the artery.

mistake.attempt: The left ventricle is much thicker than the right, so it must pump considerably more blood.
mistake.diagnosis: Thickness and volume are being treated as the same measurement. The two ventricles sit in series, so over any sustained period they must move the same volume — otherwise blood would accumulate in one circuit. The extra muscle reflects the pressure the left side generates, not extra volume.
mistake.repair: Both ventricles move about 5 L/min. The left does it against roughly 120/80 mmHg; the right against roughly 25/10 mmHg.
mistake.check: Suppose the left pumped 10 % more than the right for ten minutes. Around half a litre would have to come from somewhere and pile up somewhere. In a closed series loop, sustained outputs have to match.

units.takeaway: The two circuits are in series, so both ventricles move the same volume per minute. Wall thickness reports the pressure each side must generate, not the volume it handles.

recall.ask: Two people have a heart rate of 110. One has a blood pressure of 125/80, the other 85/50. What does the second pairing add that the heart rate alone did not?
recall.answer: That the fast rate has not succeeded in holding the pressure up. The pairing suggests the circulation is compensating and not fully keeping pace, which a single rate of 110 could never distinguish from fright or exertion.

units.title: What a blood pressure number is measuring
units.goal: Relate pressure, flow and resistance, and compute mean arterial pressure from a cuff reading.
opening: A cuff reading of 120/80 gives two numbers: the peak pressure while the left ventricle ejects, and the pressure that remains between beats. Neither is the average, and neither is the flow.
The relationship that ties them together is the same one that governs any fluid in a pipe: pressure is what you get when you push a flow through a resistance.
units.heading: One pressure, two possible causes
teaching: Write it as pressure ≈ flow × resistance. In the circulation, mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance. Because two terms multiply to give one result, a single pressure reading cannot tell you which term produced it.

The mean is not the midpoint of the two cuff numbers, because the heart spends more of each cycle relaxed than ejecting. A good approximation is the diastolic pressure plus one third of the difference between the two: MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3.
terms: Systolic minus diastolic — the size of the swing with each beat.
The average pressure over the whole cardiac cycle, weighted toward diastole.
How hard the circulation as a whole resists flow, set mostly by small arteries.

first.title: From a cuff reading to a mean
first.problem: A blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Find the pulse pressure and the mean arterial pressure.
steps: This is the swing produced by each ejection, not an average of anything.
At rest roughly one third of the cycle is spent ejecting and two thirds relaxed, so the mean sits nearer the diastolic value.
Note that the midpoint, 100 mmHg, would have overestimated it.
Say what the mean is for
Mean pressure drives steady flow to organs
Organs are perfused across the whole cycle, so the time-weighted average is the number that matters for delivery.
first.notice: At fast heart rates diastole shortens more than systole does, so the one-third approximation becomes less accurate.

second.title: Same pressure, two different states
second.problem: Two people both have a mean arterial pressure near 93 mmHg. In one, cardiac output is high and vessels are wide; in the other, output is low and vessels are tight. Can the cuff tell them apart?
steps: One number on the left, two on the right. The equation cannot be solved for both from one measurement.
High CO × low SVR ≈ low CO × high SVR
Both products can land on 93. The cuff reports only the product.
Other observations: skin warmth, pulse character, urine output
Separating the terms requires information beyond the pressure itself.
second.notice: This is the general shape of the problem: one measurement, two unknowns. It recurs whenever a reading is a product.

exercise: A blood pressure is 160/70 mmHg. Find the pulse pressure and the mean arterial pressure, and say which is unusual.

Pulse pressure = 160 − 70 = 90 mmHg; MAP ≈ 70 + 90/3 = 100 mmHg. The mean is only modestly raised while the pulse pressure is wide, which points at a large swing per beat rather than a uniformly high pressure.

mistake.attempt: Blood pressure tells you how much blood is flowing — a higher pressure means more flow.
mistake.diagnosis: Pressure and flow are different quantities linked by resistance. Since pressure ≈ flow × resistance, a high pressure can arise from a high flow through ordinary vessels, or from an ordinary flow through narrowed ones. The reading is the product, so it cannot report either factor by itself.
mistake.repair: Read a pressure as the product of two terms, and ask which one you have evidence about.
mistake.check: Think about a garden hose. Pinching the nozzle raises the pressure upstream while the flow coming out falls. If pressure measured flow, that could not happen.

units.takeaway: Pressure ≈ flow × resistance, so one pressure reading cannot tell you which term produced it. MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3, not the midpoint.

recall.ask: Why can the right ventricle drive the same 5 L/min as the left with only about a fifth of the pressure?
recall.answer: Because pressure ≈ flow × resistance, and the pulmonary circuit is a short, wide, low-resistance bed. The same flow through a much lower resistance needs much less pressure to drive it.

units.title: Why lungs are built as millions of tiny sacs
units.goal: Use area, gradient and thickness to predict how fast a gas crosses a membrane.
opening: Air reaching the end of the airways arrives in alveoli: small, thin-walled sacs wrapped in capillaries. There are a few hundred million of them, and together their surface is comparable to a badminton court folded into the chest.

That design is not decoration. The rate at which a gas crosses a membrane depends on how much surface is available, how steep the gradient is, and how far the gas has to travel — and the lung is built to make the first large, the second usable, and the third very small.
units.heading: Three terms, and only one of them is breathing
teaching: Transfer rate rises with surface area and with the partial-pressure difference, and falls as the barrier thickens. The alveolar wall and capillary wall together are under a micrometre across, which is why a gas can equilibrate in the fraction of a second a red cell spends passing one alveolus.

Because three separate terms set the rate, it matters which one is limiting. Disease that destroys alveolar walls removes area; fluid between alveolus and capillary increases the distance; a blocked airway removes the gradient by stopping fresh gas arriving. Each has a different consequence, and more breathing does not fix all three equally.
terms: The share of total gas pressure contributed by one gas; the gradient that drives its diffusion.
A thin-walled air sac where gas meets blood.
The total membrane available for exchange — roughly 70 m² in an adult lung.

first.title: Why many small sacs beat one large bag
first.problem: Compare the exchange surface of roughly 300 million alveoli with a single sphere of the same total volume, about 3 litres.
steps: Each alveolus is tiny, but there are hundreds of millions of them, and surface adds up faster than volume when you subdivide.
A 3 L sphere has a radius near 9 cm and a surface near 0.1 m²
Same volume of air, about seven hundred times less membrane.
Rate ∝ area, so area is the dominant design variable
Subdividing the same volume is the cheapest way to multiply exchange surface.
Check the other two terms are protected
Thin walls, and fresh gas delivered each breath
Subdivision would be wasted if the barrier were thick or the gradient were allowed to run down.
first.notice: Breathing restores the gradient; the alveolar architecture supplies the area. They are separate jobs done by separate parts of the design.

second.title: What happens when the distance grows
second.problem: Fluid collects between the alveolus and the capillary, roughly doubling the distance a gas must cross. The gradient and the area are unchanged. What happens to transfer?
steps: Thickness up; area and gradient unchanged
Only one of the three terms has moved.
Roughly doubling the path roughly halves the transfer for the same gradient.
Oxygen is affected more than carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide is far more soluble and diffuses much more readily, so a thickened barrier impairs oxygen transfer first.
second.notice: That asymmetry is informative: a person can have a low oxygen level while clearing carbon dioxide perfectly well.

exercise: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, merging many small sacs into fewer large ones. The total lung volume may be unchanged or even larger. Why does exchange still fall?

Because merging sacs destroys surface area even while preserving volume — the same relationship that made subdivision valuable, running backwards. Rate depends on area, not on how much air the lung can hold.

mistake.attempt: If someone's oxygen level is low, breathing harder and faster will always bring it back up.
mistake.diagnosis: Ventilation is only one of the three terms. If area has been destroyed or the barrier has thickened, moving more air past the same damaged membrane adds little. Extra ventilation also clears carbon dioxide far more effectively than it loads oxygen, because blood leaving healthy alveoli is already almost fully saturated and cannot carry much more.
mistake.repair: Ask which term is limiting: the gradient, the area, or the distance. Only a gradient problem responds well to more breathing.
mistake.check: Note that the two gases respond differently to identical extra ventilation. If breathing were the only term that mattered, oxygen and carbon dioxide would move together.

units.takeaway: Transfer rises with area and gradient and falls with thickness. Breathing only restores the gradient, which is why more of it does not fix a problem of lost area or added distance.

recall.ask: A blood pressure is 100/40 mmHg. Find the pulse pressure and the mean arterial pressure.
recall.answer: Pulse pressure = 100 − 40 = 60 mmHg. MAP ≈ 40 + 60/3 = 60 mmHg. The midpoint, 70, would again have overestimated the mean.

units.title: Filter everything, then take back what you need
units.goal: Explain why selectivity lives in reabsorption, and use a transport maximum to predict when a substance appears in urine.
opening: The intuitive design for a kidney would be a sieve that picks out the waste and lets everything valuable stay in the blood. That is not how it works.

The glomerulus filters almost indiscriminately: water, salts, glucose, amino acids and wastes all cross together. The selectivity comes afterwards, in a long tubule that reclaims what the body wants and lets the rest go.
units.heading: Why a wasteful-looking design is the flexible one
teaching: About 180 litres are filtered each day and about 1.5 litres leave as urine, so more than 99 % of the filtrate is reabsorbed. Filtering far more than you intend to excrete looks wasteful, but it means the amount of anything removed can be adjusted continuously by changing how much is taken back, rather than by rebuilding the filter.

Reabsorption uses transporters, and transporters can be saturated. Each substance has a transport maximum: a rate above which the carriers are all occupied and the excess continues into the urine. That threshold behaviour is why some substances are absent from urine until a blood level is crossed, then appear rapidly.
terms: Non-selective movement of plasma into the tubule at the glomerulus.
Selective return of filtered substances from the tubule to the blood.
The highest rate at which carriers can reabsorb a substance.

first.title: How much comes back
first.problem: 180 litres are filtered in a day and 1.5 litres are passed as urine. What fraction is reabsorbed, and why filter so much?
steps: Almost everything that crossed the filter is taken back.
Less than one per cent of the filtrate leaves the body.
Ask why the design is worth it
Excretion is tuned by adjusting reabsorption
Because the filter is non-selective and generous, fine control of any one substance is a matter of changing how much is reclaimed.
Urine output can vary from well under 1 L to several litres a day
That range comes from varying reabsorption, not from varying the filter.
first.notice: A selective filter would have to be rebuilt to change its behaviour. A generous filter plus adjustable reabsorption can be retuned minute to minute.

second.title: Glucose and a saturated transporter
second.problem: Glucose is filtered freely yet healthy urine contains almost none. What has to happen before glucose appears?
steps: At ordinary blood levels the transporters keep up completely, so none is lost.
Reabsorption rate rises with the filtered load only until every carrier is occupied.
Above the threshold, the excess stays in the tubule and is excreted
Glucose then appears in urine, and because it holds water osmotically it drags volume with it.
second.notice: The osmotic effect explains a classic pairing: large urine volumes and thirst arriving together once the threshold is crossed.

exercise: Why does the body filter around 180 litres a day only to reabsorb more than 99 % of it? Give the functional reason rather than restating the numbers.

Because a generous, non-selective filter combined with adjustable reabsorption gives fine, fast control over every solute independently. Excretion of any substance can be changed by altering how much is taken back, without redesigning the filter.

mistake.attempt: The kidney picks the waste out of the blood and removes it, leaving the useful substances behind.
mistake.diagnosis: That reverses the design. Filtration at the glomerulus is close to indiscriminate — glucose, amino acids, salts and water all cross along with urea. Selectivity is applied afterwards, by reclaiming what is wanted. The kidney decides what to *keep*, not what to remove.
mistake.repair: Describe it in two stages: filter generously, then reabsorb selectively. 180 litres filtered, about 1.5 litres excreted.
mistake.check: Glucose makes the design visible. It is filtered freely and then fully reabsorbed, which is why healthy urine contains almost none — and why it appears as soon as the blood level exceeds what the transporters can reclaim.

units.takeaway: The glomerulus filters almost everything; the tubule reclaims what is wanted. Selectivity lives in reabsorption, and saturable transporters give threshold behaviour.

recall.ask: Fluid thickens the barrier between alveolus and capillary. Why does oxygen transfer suffer more than carbon dioxide transfer?
recall.answer: Carbon dioxide is much more soluble and diffuses far more readily, so it tolerates a longer path. A thickened barrier therefore shows up as a low oxygen level while carbon dioxide clearance may still be adequate.

units.title: A control loop that can fail in two ways
units.goal: Read a hormone and its target variable together, and distinguish a weak signal from a weak response.
opening: Blood glucose is held in a narrow band by a loop you already know the shape of: a sensor, a set point, and effectors that push in either direction. Insulin lowers glucose; glucagon raises it.

What makes this loop worth a unit of its own is that it can fail in two quite different places — the signal can be too small, or the response to a normal signal can be too weak — and the two look different only if you read both numbers.
units.heading: The output of a controller is not the state of the system
teaching: After a meal, glucose rises, beta cells release insulin, tissues take glucose up and store it, and glucose returns toward the set point. Insulin here is the controller's output: a measure of how hard the system is pushing.

If tissues respond poorly to insulin, the loop compensates by pushing harder, so insulin rises. Glucose may stay near normal for a long time on the strength of that extra push, and then drift up as the compensation stops being enough. Insulin high with glucose high is therefore a coherent state, not a contradiction — it says the signal is loud and the response is weak.
terms: Hormone released when glucose rises; moves glucose into cells and promotes storage.
Reduced tissue response to a given amount of insulin.
A larger controller output that holds the regulated variable steady despite a weaker response.

first.title: The loop working normally
first.problem: Glucose rises after a meal and is back in range two hours later. Name each element of the loop and the direction it pushes.
steps: Glucose above set point → positive error
The same first step as any regulated variable.
Insulin is the correcting action, released in proportion to the size of the error.
Uptake into muscle and fat; storage as glycogen in liver
Glucose leaves the blood compartment. The measured variable falls.
Glucose falls → error shrinks → insulin release eases
Self-limiting, like every negative feedback loop.
first.notice: Insulin falling after a meal is not the loop weakening. It is the loop succeeding.

second.title: A weak response, read two ways
second.problem: Two people both have a fasting glucose at the top of the usual range. One has a low-normal insulin level, the other a markedly high one. What differs?
steps: A modest push is producing a modest result. The response to insulin appears intact.
A large push is needed to achieve the same glucose, which points at a weakened tissue response.
Say what one number would have missed
The glucose values are nearly identical
Reading glucose alone makes the two look the same. The difference is entirely in the controller's effort.
second.notice: This is the same lesson as pressure ≈ flow × resistance: when a result comes from two factors, one measurement cannot separate them.

exercise: Someone's insulin level is well above normal while their glucose sits in the upper part of the usual range. Does the high insulin reassure you that glucose control is working well?

No. It says the loop is pushing hard. Glucose is being held only by an unusually large signal, which is the picture of a weak tissue response rather than a healthy one. Read the pair: the effort and the result.

mistake.attempt: Insulin lowers blood glucose, so if someone's insulin is high their glucose must be low.
mistake.diagnosis: That assumes a signal always produces its intended effect. The level of a controller's output tells you how hard the system is working, not whether the work is succeeding. In insulin resistance the pancreas raises output precisely because tissues respond poorly, so high insulin and high glucose occur together.
mistake.repair: Read the controller output and the regulated variable as a pair: insulin says how hard, glucose says whether it worked.
mistake.check: Picture a thermostat driving a failing heater. A maximum output signal together with a cold room is perfectly consistent — and it tells you the fault is in the heater, not the thermostat.

units.takeaway: A hormone level is a controller output, not a verdict on the system. High signal with an off-target variable means the signal is loud and the response is weak.

recall.ask: Why does glucose appear in urine only once blood glucose passes a threshold, rather than in proportion to it all the way down?
recall.answer: Because reabsorption uses saturable transporters. Below the transport maximum every filtered glucose molecule is reclaimed, so none appears. Once the carriers are fully occupied the excess stays in the tubule, so excretion begins abruptly at a threshold.

units.title: Fast and general, then slow and specific
units.goal: Contrast innate and adaptive responses by speed, specificity and memory, and explain why a drug needs a target.
opening: Defence against infection runs on two systems with different trade-offs. One is ready immediately and treats all intruders roughly alike. The other takes days to organise, is precisely matched to one target, and remembers.

Almost everything that seems puzzling about infection and vaccination follows from that pairing: why a first illness lasts longer than a second, why vaccines work, and why some drugs help with one kind of organism and not another.
units.heading: Speed and specificity pull in opposite directions
teaching: Innate defences — skin, mucus, stomach acid, and cells that engulf anything recognisably foreign — act within minutes. They are general, which is what allows them to be fast: there is no need to identify the organism first. They also do not improve with exposure.

Adaptive defences select and multiply the small number of lymphocytes that happen to match the intruder, which takes days on a first encounter. The pay-off is memory: matched cells persist, so a second exposure is met in hours rather than days. A vaccine supplies the first encounter without the illness.
terms: Immediate, general defence with no memory.
Slower, specific defence that leaves lasting memory.
A structure a drug can act on that the pathogen has and we do not.

first.title: First exposure against second exposure
first.problem: The same organism is met twice, years apart. Sketch the time course of each response.
steps: Barriers and engulfing cells act at once. They slow the infection without clearing it.
Days three to ten, first exposure
Matching lymphocytes are selected and multiply. Illness is typically at its worst while this is still being assembled.
The selection step has already happened, so the slow part of the first response is skipped.
The difference is timing, not strength of the final response.
first.notice: Vaccination moves the slow step earlier in time, so that the first real encounter behaves like a second.

second.title: What a drug has to grab hold of
second.problem: An antibiotic stops bacteria building cell walls. Why does that spare human cells, and what does it predict about viruses?
steps: Bacteria build a peptidoglycan wall; human cells have no such structure.
The drug acts on something we do not possess
Selective toxicity comes from a difference between the pathogen and us, not from the drug being gentle.
Viruses have no cell wall and no bacterial ribosome
There is no structure for this class of drug to act on, so it has no effect on a viral illness.
second.notice: Asking 'what does this drug bind to, and do I have one?' predicts both the usefulness and the side effects.

exercise: Why is a second infection with the same organism usually milder and shorter than the first?

Because the slow part of the first response — selecting and multiplying matching lymphocytes — has already been done. Memory cells persist, so the specific response arrives in hours instead of days and the infection is contained before it causes as much illness.

mistake.attempt: This cold has dragged on for a week, so an antibiotic should clear it up.
mistake.diagnosis: Antibiotics act on bacterial machinery: cell-wall synthesis, bacterial ribosomes, bacterial folate production. Colds are caused by viruses, which have none of those structures, so there is nothing for the drug to act on. Duration does not change what the organism is.
mistake.repair: Match the agent to a target the organism actually has. Viral illnesses are cleared by the adaptive response, on its own timetable.
mistake.check: Ask what the drug binds to, and whether the organism has it. If you cannot name the structure, there is no reason to expect an effect. (This unit explains mechanism; decisions about treating any real person belong with a clinician.)

units.takeaway: Innate defence is fast, general and memoryless; adaptive defence is slow, specific and remembers. A drug works only where the pathogen has a structure we lack.

recall.ask: Someone has a high insulin level and a glucose level in the upper part of the usual range. What does the pair say that glucose alone could not?
recall.answer: That glucose is being held in range only by an unusually large controller output. The signal is loud and the tissue response is weak — a different state from the same glucose achieved with a modest insulin level.

units.title: Half-life, and how much is still there
units.goal: Compute the amount remaining after n half-lives and explain what changing the dose does and does not change.
opening: Most drugs are cleared in a way that removes a constant *fraction* per unit time rather than a constant amount. Half-life is the time for the amount in the body to fall by half.
That one property decides a surprising amount: how long an effect lasts, how often a dose has to be repeated, and how long it takes before repeated dosing settles at a steady level.
units.heading: Counting half-lives instead of hours
teaching: After n half-lives the fraction remaining is (½)ⁿ. After one half-life, 50 % remains; after two, 25 %; after four, 6.25 %. The convenience of this is that the fraction does not depend on the starting amount — only the number of half-lives elapsed.

Dose size and dose interval do different jobs. The dose sets how high the level goes; the interval sets how far it falls before the next one. With repeated dosing the level climbs toward a plateau and is close to it after about four to five half-lives, which is also roughly how long it takes to wash out after stopping.
terms: Time for the amount in the body to fall by half.
A constant fraction removed per unit time, which is what makes half-life constant.
The plateau reached with repeated dosing, after roughly four to five half-lives.

first.title: How much is left after a day
first.problem: A 400 mg dose is given. The half-life is 6 hours. How much remains after 24 hours?
steps: Always convert the time into half-lives before doing anything else.
One halving per half-life, at 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours.
The fraction route and the step-by-step route must agree.
The 400 mg played no part in finding the fraction
The fraction remaining depends only on elapsed half-lives.
first.notice: Writing the halvings out is slower but makes the pattern visible, which matters for the next example.

second.title: Building up to a steady level
second.problem: The same drug is given every 6 hours. Why does the level climb and then stop climbing?
steps: Dose 400 mg; 6 hours later 200 mg remains
Half has gone, so half of the dose is still present when the next one arrives.
200 + 400 = 600 mg, falling to 300 before the next
Each dose lands on a residue, so the peaks rise.
It plateaus when the amount cleared per interval equals the dose given
As the level rises, a constant fraction of a larger amount is a larger absolute removal. Eventually removal per interval matches the dose.
Close to the plateau after about 4–5 half-lives
Here, roughly 24–30 hours of regular dosing.
second.notice: Washing out after stopping takes about the same 4–5 half-lives, for exactly the same reason running in reverse.

exercise: A drug with a 3-hour half-life is given as a 600 mg dose. How much remains after 12 hours, and what fraction is that?
12 ÷ 3 = 4 half-lives. 600 → 300 → 150 → 75 → 37.5 mg. That is (½)⁴ = 1/16 = 6.25 % of the starting amount.

mistake.attempt: Doubling the dose will make the drug last twice as long.
mistake.diagnosis: Half-life does not depend on the starting amount. Doubling the dose does not double the time to reach any given level — it adds exactly one extra halving, which is one half-life, however large the dose.
mistake.repair: From 400 mg with a 6-hour half-life, 25 mg is reached at 24 hours. From 800 mg it is reached at 30 hours: six hours later, not twenty-four. Controlling the level between doses is a matter of the interval, not the dose size.
mistake.check: Count halvings. 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 is five steps at 6 hours each. Each doubling of the dose buys one more fixed-length half-life, never a doubling of duration.

units.takeaway: After n half-lives, (½)ⁿ remains, independent of the starting dose. Dose sets the height, interval sets the trough, and steady state arrives after about four to five half-lives.

recall.ask: Why does an antibiotic that blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis have no effect on a cold?
recall.answer: Because colds are viral and viruses have no cell wall for the drug to act on. Selective toxicity depends on the pathogen possessing a structure we lack; with no target present, there is no mechanism for an effect.

units.title: Why a positive test is not a diagnosis
units.goal: Compute predictive value from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence, and explain why prevalence changes the answer.
opening: A test described as 99 % sensitive and 95 % specific sounds close to decisive. Applied to a condition that affects one person in a hundred, a positive result from it is wrong more often than it is right.

Nothing about that is a trick. It follows from the fact that the false positives are drawn from a much larger group than the true positives, and the only reliable way to see it is to count people rather than reason about percentages.
units.heading: Two conditional probabilities pointing in opposite directions
teaching: Sensitivity is the proportion of people *with* the condition who test positive. Specificity is the proportion *without* it who test negative. Both are conditioned on knowing the true state — which is the thing a patient does not know.

Predictive value runs the other way: given a positive result, how likely is the condition? That depends on sensitivity, specificity and how common the condition is. Because the people without the condition can vastly outnumber those with it, even a small false-positive rate can generate more false positives than there are true ones.
terms: Of those who have it, the fraction testing positive.
Of those who do not, the fraction testing negative.
Of those testing positive, the fraction who really have it.

first.title: Counting a rare condition
first.problem: Sensitivity 99 %, specificity 95 %, prevalence 1 %. Out of 10,000 people, how trustworthy is a positive result?
steps: Split the population by true state
Always start by splitting on the truth, not on the test.
Apply sensitivity to the affected group
One person with the condition is missed.
Apply specificity to the unaffected group
A 95 % specificity sounds high, but 5 % of a large group is a large number.
Fewer than one positive result in five is correct, from a test with excellent-sounding properties.
first.notice: The 495 false positives come from a group 99 times larger than the affected one. That size difference is doing all the work.

second.title: The same test where the condition is common
second.problem: Keep sensitivity at 99 % and specificity at 95 %, but raise prevalence to 30 %. Recompute.
steps: Only the split has changed. The test is identical.
The unaffected group is now much smaller, so it produces far fewer false positives.
Same test, same numbers on the box, utterly different meaning for the person holding the result.
second.notice: This is why the same test means one thing in a screening programme and another in someone already likely to have the condition.

exercise: A test is 90 % sensitive and 90 % specific, and the condition affects 2 % of those tested. Out of 10,000 people, what fraction of positive results are correct?

200 have it: 90 % gives 180 true positives. 9,800 do not: 10 % gives 980 false positives. Predictive value = 180 ÷ 1,160 = 15.5 %. Most positives are wrong, because the unaffected group is 49 times larger.

mistake.attempt: The test is 99 % accurate, so a positive result means I almost certainly have the condition.
mistake.diagnosis: Sensitivity is a conditional probability in the opposite direction to the one being used. It describes what the test does to people who already have the condition; it says nothing by itself about people who test positive. When the condition is rare, the false positives are drawn from a far larger group and can easily outnumber the true ones.
mistake.repair: At 1 % prevalence with 99 % sensitivity and 95 % specificity, 10,000 people yield 99 true positives and 495 false ones, so a positive is right about 17 % of the time.
mistake.check: Work in counts, not percentages. Write out the four cells for 10,000 people and the answer stops depending on intuition entirely.

units.takeaway: Sensitivity and specificity are conditioned on the true state; predictive value is conditioned on the result. Prevalence decides which one dominates, so count people in a 2×2 table rather than reasoning in percentages.

recall.ask: A 200 mg dose has an 8-hour half-life. How much remains after 32 hours?
recall.answer: 32 ÷ 8 = 4 half-lives, so 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5 mg. That is (½)⁴ = 6.25 % of the dose.

project.title: Follow the oxygen: air, blood, tissue, and what a test adds
project.intro: One quantity tracked across four stages: from the air in the room to the oxygen actually delivered to tissue each minute, and then what a normal-looking reading can hide. Every step is calculated with standard values, and each one uses a different unit from the course.
project.needs: Uses gas exchange, the two circuits, blood pressure and test interpretation. Standard reference values and a resting adult are assumed throughout. This is an explanation of mechanism, not clinical guidance.

parts.title: From room air to the alveolus
parts.goal: Compute the oxygen pressure actually available at the exchange surface.
opening: Room air is about 21 % oxygen at a total pressure near 760 mmHg. That does not mean the alveolus sees 21 % of 760, because two things happen to the air on the way in: it is fully humidified, and it mixes with gas already there that is loaded with carbon dioxide.
I will take both into account before anything crosses a membrane, because the gradient computed here is what drives every later step.

steps.title: Remove the water vapour first
steps.explanation: Air is fully saturated with water by the time it reaches the alveoli, and at body temperature water vapour contributes about 47 mmHg. That share is unavailable to the other gases.

steps.title: Take oxygen's share
steps.explanation: This is inspired oxygen pressure at the airway, after humidification but before any exchange has occurred.

steps.title: Account for the carbon dioxide present
steps.explanation: Alveolar gas continuously receives carbon dioxide from blood, and that occupies pressure. Dividing by the respiratory quotient of about 0.8 accounts for slightly less oxygen being consumed than carbon dioxide produced, per unit volume.

steps.title: Read off the gradient
steps.work: Alveolus 100 mmHg vs arriving blood 40 mmHg
steps.explanation: A 60 mmHg difference drives diffusion. This is the gradient term from the gas-exchange unit, now with a number attached.

parts.ending: The alveolus sees about 100 mmHg, not 160. Humidification and resident carbon dioxide account for the difference.

parts.title: From alveolus into the blood
parts.goal: Turn an oxygen pressure into the amount of oxygen a volume of blood actually carries.
opening: Pressure and content are different quantities. The 100 mmHg we just computed is a pressure; what matters for delivery is how many millilitres of oxygen each 100 mL of blood is carrying.
Almost all of it rides on haemoglobin. Only a small amount is dissolved, and keeping that separate is what makes the next stage come out right.

steps.title: Convert pressure to saturation
steps.explanation: The relationship is a curve, not a line, and it is nearly flat above about 80 mmHg. That flatness is why extra ventilation adds very little oxygen to blood already leaving healthy alveoli.

steps.title: Compute the bound oxygen
steps.explanation: Each gram of haemoglobin carries about 1.34 mL of oxygen when fully saturated. With a haemoglobin of 15 g/dL this is the overwhelming majority of the total.

steps.title: Add the dissolved fraction
steps.explanation: Dissolved oxygen is small enough to ignore in most reasoning, which is itself the point: content tracks haemoglobin far more than it tracks pressure.

steps.title: Total the content
steps.explanation: Twenty millilitres of oxygen per 100 mL of blood, essentially all of it carried rather than dissolved.

parts.ending: Content is about 20 mL/dL, and roughly 98 % of it is bound to haemoglobin rather than dissolved.

parts.title: From blood to tissue
parts.goal: Combine flow and content into oxygen delivered per minute.
opening: Delivery is a rate, so it needs a flow as well as a content. This is where the circulation units join the respiratory ones.
The structure is the same product we met with pressure: two factors multiplying into one result, which means a single normal-looking factor cannot guarantee a normal result.

steps.title: Write the product
steps.explanation: Flow in litres per minute, content in millilitres per decilitre. The units need reconciling before multiplying.

steps.title: Fix the units
steps.explanation: There are 10 decilitres in a litre, so the factor of 10 converts content per decilitre into content per litre.

steps.title: Compute delivery
steps.explanation: About a litre of oxygen delivered each minute at rest.

steps.title: Compare with consumption
steps.work: Resting use ≈ 250 mL/min, about a quarter of delivery
steps.explanation: The reserve is what allows demand to rise several-fold before delivery becomes limiting — and what allows a problem to be invisible at rest.

parts.ending: Delivery ≈ 1,000 mL/min against a resting demand near 250 mL/min, leaving roughly a four-fold reserve.

parts.title: A normal reading over a halved delivery
parts.goal: Show why one measurement cannot stand in for a product, and what a test result adds.
opening: Now change one input. Suppose haemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL instead of 15, with everything else — lungs, saturation, cardiac output — unchanged.
I will recompute with the same sequence rather than inventing a new method, then ask what a measurement would and would not reveal.

steps.title: Recompute the content
steps.explanation: Halving the carrier roughly halves the content. Nothing about the lungs has changed.

steps.title: Recompute delivery
steps.explanation: Delivery has roughly halved, and the resting demand of 250 mL/min is now about half of supply rather than a quarter.

steps.title: Ask what a pulse oximeter would show
steps.explanation: Saturation is the percentage of available haemoglobin that is loaded, not how much haemoglobin there is. A normal saturation over a halved carrier is entirely consistent.

steps.title: Say what the reading can and cannot settle
steps.work: Normal saturation rules out one term, not the product
steps.explanation: This is the structure from the blood-pressure unit again: one measurement, more than one unknown. The reassuring number addresses only the factor it measures.

parts.ending: Delivery can halve while the saturation reading stays at 98 %. A measurement constrains the factor it measures — never the whole product.

workshop.title: Watch a teacher read the evidence
workshop.summary: Four readings: a number with its partner, a measurement that cannot settle a product, finding the limiting term, and counting people instead of percentages.
workshop.intro: Four short cases where the hard part is deciding what a measurement can and cannot tell you. In each one I state what the number settles, what it leaves open, and what a second number would add.
workshop.needs: Use after the vital signs, pressure, gas exchange and test units. These are worked readings of measurements, not clinical guidance about any real person.

parts.title: A number and its partner
parts.goal: See how a second reading changes what the first one means.
opening: Two people both have a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. On its own that number is compatible with fright, exertion, fever, pain and serious blood loss.
I will add one more measurement to each and watch the interpretations separate — without the heart rate itself changing at all.

steps.title: Start with the unpaired number
steps.why: A heart rate alone names no cause. Reference ranges describe a population, so being outside one is a prompt to look further rather than a conclusion.

steps.title: Add a blood pressure to the first
steps.why: The pressure is being held up. A fast rate with a maintained pressure is consistent with an ordinary stressor — the circulation is not failing to deliver.

steps.title: Add a blood pressure to the second
steps.why: Here the fast rate has not succeeded in holding the pressure. That pattern suggests the heart is compensating and not fully keeping pace — a different situation entirely.

steps.title: Add the direction of travel
steps.line: 80 → 95 → 110 is not the same as 110 held steady for a year.
steps.why: Baseline and trend are the third and fourth pieces. A reading becomes information only once you know what is usual for this person and which way it is moving.

parts.ending: The same 110 carried opposite weight in the two cases. The information lived in the pairing and the trend, never in the single number.

parts.title: When one reading cannot settle a product
parts.goal: Recognise the shape of a measurement that is the product of two unknowns.
opening: Several of the body's most-quoted numbers are products. Mean arterial pressure is roughly cardiac output times resistance; oxygen delivery is cardiac output times content.
One measurement of a product can never report both factors. I will work that through twice, then show the same shape in a hormone level.

steps.title: Write the first product
steps.line: MAP ≈ CO × SVR, and 80 + 40/3 = 93 mmHg from a 120/80 cuff
steps.why: A mean of 93 can come from a high output through wide vessels or an ordinary output through tight ones. The cuff reports only the product.

steps.title: Write the second product
steps.why: Halve the haemoglobin and content falls to about 10 mL/dL, so delivery falls to about 510 mL/min — while saturation still reads 98 %, because saturation measures the fraction loaded, not how much carrier there is.

steps.title: Find the same shape in a hormone
steps.line: Glucose high-normal with insulin low vs with insulin high
steps.why: Insulin is the controller's effort and glucose is the result. Identical glucose values with very different insulin levels describe two different states, and glucose alone cannot separate them.

steps.title: State the general move
steps.line: One equation, two unknowns → find a second measurement.
steps.why: Whenever a reading is a product, the useful question is which factor you have independent evidence about. A reassuring number constrains only the factor it measures.

parts.ending: Pressure, delivery and glucose control are all products. A single normal-looking reading rules out one factor, never the whole product.

parts.title: Which term is limiting?
parts.goal: Decide which of three terms a proposed intervention actually changes.
opening: Gas transfer rises with surface area and with the pressure gradient, and falls as the barrier thickens. Three terms, and breathing changes only one of them.
I will take three different causes of a low oxygen level and ask, for each, whether more ventilation would help.

steps.title: Write the relationship
steps.why: Naming the three terms before reasoning is what stops every respiratory problem being treated as the same problem.

steps.title: A gradient problem
steps.line: Less fresh gas reaching the alveoli → gradient falls
steps.why: This is the one term ventilation directly restores, so more breathing is the matching response.

steps.title: An area problem
steps.line: Alveolar walls destroyed; volume unchanged or larger
steps.why: Merging many small sacs into fewer large ones destroys surface while preserving volume. Moving more air past a smaller membrane adds little.

steps.title: A thickness problem
steps.line: Fluid roughly doubles the path → transfer roughly halves
steps.why: Oxygen suffers more than carbon dioxide, which is far more soluble. A low oxygen level with adequate carbon dioxide clearance is a hint that the barrier, not the ventilation, is the limiting term.

parts.ending: Three causes, one symptom, and only the first responds well to more breathing. The asymmetry between the two gases is the clue that distinguishes them.

parts.title: Count people, not percentages
parts.goal: Work a predictive value twice and watch prevalence decide the answer.
opening: A test is 99 % sensitive and 95 % specific. Those numbers do not change in this chapter. The only thing that changes is how common the condition is.
I will lay out the four cells for 10,000 people each time, because percentages are exactly where intuition fails here.

steps.title: Split on the truth first
steps.line: At 1 % prevalence: 100 have it, 9,900 do not.
steps.why: Splitting on the true state rather than on the result is what makes the asymmetry visible. The second group is 99 times larger.

steps.title: Fill the cells
steps.why: A 95 % specificity sounds excellent, but five per cent of a very large group is a large number of people.

steps.title: Read off the predictive value
steps.why: Fewer than one positive in five is correct — from a test whose stated properties look close to decisive.

steps.title: Change only the prevalence
steps.why: Same test, same two percentages on the box, and a completely different meaning for the person holding the result. This is why screening and confirming are different jobs.

parts.ending: Sensitivity is conditioned on having the condition; predictive value is conditioned on the result. Prevalence decides which dominates, and counting people settles it.

business.subject: business
business.title: How a business actually makes money
business.intro: Eleven units built on one running example: unit economics, breakeven, the cash cycle, pricing, what a customer is worth, and why a profitable month can still empty the bank account.

stages.title: What one sale actually leaves you
stages.goal: Separate profit from cash, and find the part of a price that is really yours.

stages.title: Cash, timing and growth
stages.goal: Why the calendar decides how much money you need, and why growth consumes it.

stages.title: Decisions and value
stages.goal: What to pay for a customer, what a discount really costs, and what a future dollar is worth.

units.title: A sale is not the same as money arriving
units.goal: Separate when revenue is earned from when cash moves, and explain how both can diverge in one month.
opening: Sunrise Oats ships 100 boxes of granola to a supermarket in March at $40 a box. The invoice says payment in 60 days. In March the company has earned $4,000 and received nothing.
Those are two different facts about the same event, and they are both true. Keeping them apart is the first skill in reading any set of accounts.
units.heading: Two clocks running on the same transaction
teaching: Revenue is recorded when the work is done and the goods are delivered — when the company has earned it. Cash is recorded when money actually moves. For a cash sale the two coincide; for anything on terms they do not.

Both measures are needed and neither replaces the other. Profit answers whether you are selling things for more than they cost you. Cash answers whether you can pay the people you owe this week. A business can pass the first test and fail the second, and failing the second is what closes the doors.
terms: The value of goods or services delivered in a period, whether or not paid for.
Money owed to you by customers for sales already made.
Cash you have taken for something you have not yet delivered.

first.title: Earned in March, paid in May
