first.problem: 100 boxes ship in March at $40 each, on 60-day terms. The oats cost $2,600 and were paid for in February. Show March's revenue and March's cash.
steps: The goods left the building in March, so March is when it was earned.
Record March's cash from this sale
The customer pays in May. Nothing has moved yet.
The ingredients were bought and paid for before the sale happened.
March profit from this sale: $1,400. Cash across Feb–Mar: −$2,600.
A profitable sale that has, so far, only consumed money.
first.notice: The $2,600 appears as a cost in March, not February, because costs are matched to the revenue they generated.

second.title: Paid in January, earned in June
second.problem: A corporate customer pays $6,000 in January for boxes to be delivered monthly through the first half of the year. What is January's revenue?
steps: The money is in the bank and can be spent.
$1,000, if one month of the six has been delivered
Revenue is recognised as the obligation is fulfilled, not when the cash lands.
It is money held against work still owed. If the company stopped trading, it would have to be returned.
second.notice: This is the mirror image of the first case: cash early and revenue late, rather than revenue early and cash late.

exercise: In April, Sunrise Oats delivers $18,000 of boxes on 30-day terms and collects $11,000 from March's deliveries. It pays $9,000 to suppliers. What is April's revenue, and what is April's cash movement?

Revenue is $18,000 — what was delivered in April. Cash movement is $11,000 collected minus $9,000 paid = +$2,000. The two numbers describe the same month and have almost nothing to do with each other.

mistake.attempt: We made $12,000 of profit last month, so there should be roughly $12,000 more in the bank than there was.
mistake.diagnosis: Profit is measured when a sale is earned; cash moves when money changes hands. A month with $12,000 of profit in which customers pay on 60-day terms and suppliers were paid on delivery can easily end with less cash than it started with.
mistake.repair: Track the two separately. Profit answers 'did we sell for more than it cost'; cash answers 'can we pay this week'.
mistake.check: A business can be profitable and unable to pay its bills at the same time — that is the ordinary way good companies fail. If profit and cash were the same measurement, that sentence would be impossible.

units.takeaway: Revenue is recorded when earned, cash when it moves. Both are needed: profit tells you whether the model works, cash tells you whether you survive long enough to find out.

recall.ask: A customer pays a $5,000 deposit in February for a delivery due in August. Where does that money sit in February, and why is it not revenue?
recall.answer: It is cash in the bank and a $5,000 liability called deferred revenue. It is not revenue because nothing has been delivered — the company still owes the work, and would have to return the money if it could not do it.

units.title: What one sale leaves behind
units.goal: Compute contribution per unit and explain what it is available to pay for.
opening: A box of Sunrise Oats sells for $40. The oats, packaging, fulfilment labour and shipping come to $26. The difference, $14, is the part of the price the company still has after making and delivering that box.
That $14 has a name — contribution — and a job: it is what is left over to pay for everything that does not vary with how many boxes you sell.
units.heading: The order in which costs get paid
teaching: Variable costs scale with volume: one more box means one more set of ingredients and one more shipping label. Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost, and it is the only part of a sale that can go toward anything else.

Fixed costs — rent, salaries, software, insurance — arrive whether or not a single box is sold. Contribution is what pays them down. Until total contribution exceeds total fixed costs the month loses money, however healthy the per-unit figure looks.
terms: A cost that rises with each additional unit sold.
A cost that does not change with volume over the period in question.
Price minus variable cost — what one sale leaves toward fixed costs and profit.

first.title: Finding the contribution
first.problem: Price $40. Oats and packaging $14, fulfilment labour $5, shipping $7. Find the contribution per box and the contribution margin.
steps: Each of these recurs with every additional box, so all three belong here.
This is what the company keeps from one sale before any fixed cost is considered.
Contribution margin is the proportion of each sale that survives the variable costs.
This is the total available to put against fixed costs — not profit.
first.notice: Contribution margin is measured against price, not against cost. That distinction returns in the margin-and-markup unit.

second.title: A small cost increase, a large effect
second.problem: A courier raises shipping from $7 to $11. Price and all other costs are unchanged. What happens?
steps: A 15 % increase in total variable cost.
A 10 % rise in one cost line has taken nearly a third of what the sale was leaving behind.
The change lands wholly on the smaller number
Contribution is a difference between two larger numbers, so changes to either hit it disproportionately.
second.notice: That leverage runs both ways, which is why small cost reductions on a thin margin are worth real effort.

exercise: Sunrise Oats launches a $25 snack pack with variable costs of $18. Find the contribution and the contribution margin, and compare with the $40 box.
Contribution is $25 − $18 = $7, a margin of 28 %. The box leaves $14 at a 35 % margin, so the snack pack needs twice the volume to contribute the same amount.

mistake.attempt: Each box earns $14, so selling 500 boxes in a month makes $7,000 of profit.
mistake.diagnosis: That is contribution, not profit. The $7,000 is what the month's sales left *toward* fixed costs — rent, salaries, software — which have to be paid whether or not anything sold.
mistake.repair: With $9,000 of monthly fixed costs, 500 boxes contribute $7,000 and the month loses $2,000.
mistake.check: Ask what happens at zero volume. Contribution goes to zero and the fixed costs do not, so the two cannot be the same quantity.

units.takeaway: Contribution = price − variable cost. It is what one sale leaves toward fixed costs, and it is not profit until the fixed costs are covered.

recall.ask: Sunrise Oats delivers $18,000 of boxes on 30-day terms in April and collects $11,000 from March. What is April's revenue?
recall.answer: $18,000 — the value delivered in April. The $11,000 collected is cash from a previous month's revenue and does not appear in April's revenue at all.

units.title: How many before the month pays for itself
units.goal: Compute breakeven volume from fixed costs and contribution, and say why price is the wrong denominator.
opening: Sunrise Oats pays $9,000 a month in rent, salaries, software and insurance before a single box ships. Each box contributes $14.
Breakeven is the volume at which those contributions have exactly covered the fixed costs — the point where the month stops losing money and starts making it.
units.heading: Divide by what is actually available
teaching: Breakeven volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit. The denominator has to be contribution, because that is the only part of each sale left over to pay a fixed cost. Using price instead assumes the whole $40 is available, when $26 of it has already been spent.

Breakeven is sensitive to contribution in a way that is easy to underestimate. Because contribution sits in the denominator, a change in it moves the required volume more than proportionally in the direction that hurts.
terms: Units needed for total contribution to equal fixed costs.
How sharply profit responds to volume, set by the fixed-to-variable mix.
How far current volume sits above breakeven.

first.title: The breakeven box count
first.problem: Fixed costs $9,000 a month. Contribution $14 a box. How many boxes to break even?
steps: At breakeven, everything the sales left over has been consumed by the fixed costs exactly.
Divide the fixed costs by what each unit actually contributes.
642 boxes contribute $8,988, which is $12 short. Breakeven volumes round up.
Multiplying back is the habit that catches a wrong denominator.
first.notice: At 643 boxes the profit is $2. Breakeven is a threshold, not a target.

second.title: When contribution falls
second.problem: The courier increase from the last unit drops contribution to $10. Fixed costs are unchanged. What is the new breakeven?
steps: A fall in the denominator raises the result more than proportionally.
Say what that means in practice
257 extra boxes a month just to stand still
None of that additional volume produces any profit; it only replaces what the cost increase removed.
second.notice: Because contribution sits in a denominator, protecting it matters more than its size alone suggests.

exercise: Fixed costs rise to $12,000 a month while contribution stays at $14. Find the new breakeven volume and check it.
12,000 ÷ 14 = 857.1, so 858 boxes. Checking: 858 × 14 = $12,012, which clears $12,000, while 857 × 14 = $11,998 falls just short.

mistake.attempt: Fixed costs are $9,000 and we sell boxes at $40, so we break even at 225 boxes.
mistake.diagnosis: That divides by the price, treating the whole $40 as available to pay rent. Most of it has already been spent on oats, packaging and shipping before the box leaves. Only the $14 of contribution is left over.
mistake.check: Multiply the wrong answer back: 225 boxes contribute 225 × $14 = $3,150, nowhere near the $9,000 of fixed costs. Multiplying back catches a wrong denominator every time.

units.takeaway: Breakeven = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit. Price is the wrong denominator, and because contribution sits underneath, protecting it moves breakeven more than its size suggests.

recall.ask: A box sells for $40 with $26 of variable cost. Give the contribution and the contribution margin, and say what the contribution is for.
recall.answer: Contribution is $14 and the margin is 14/40 = 35 %. It is what one sale leaves toward fixed costs; it only becomes profit once the fixed costs for the period are fully covered.

units.title: Average cost is an answer, not an input
units.goal: Separate fixed from variable costs and explain why cost per unit falls as volume rises.
opening: Ask what a box of Sunrise Oats costs to make and you can get two defensible answers: $26, or $44. Both come from the same accounts.

The difference is whether you have folded a share of the fixed costs into the figure — and if you have, at what volume. That makes average cost per unit a result of an assumption, not a fact about the box.
units.heading: The fixed share moves even when nothing else does
teaching: Variable cost per unit is stable: $26 of oats, packaging, labour and shipping, whether you make 10 boxes or 10,000. Fixed cost per unit is not, because the same $9,000 is divided among however many boxes there are.

So total cost = fixed + (variable × volume), and average cost = that total divided by volume. The average falls as volume rises purely because the fixed share is spread thinner — nothing about the production has become more efficient.
terms: Fixed costs plus variable cost per unit times volume.
Total cost divided by volume — dependent on the volume assumed.
A cost that is fixed within a range and jumps when capacity is exceeded.

first.title: The same business at two volumes
first.problem: Fixed costs $9,000 a month, variable cost $26 a box. Find total and average cost at 500 boxes and at 1,000.
steps: The fixed block plus the variable block.
This is where the $44 figure comes from: it embeds $18 of fixed cost per box.
The fixed share has halved to $9 a box, so the average fell by $9.
first.notice: Nothing got cheaper to produce. The $26 never moved; only the denominator under the $9,000 did.

second.title: A fixed cost that is not flat forever
second.problem: The current oven handles 800 boxes a month. Going beyond it means a second oven at $2,000 a month. What does cost look like at 850 boxes?
steps: Fixed costs are only fixed within a capacity range.
The step lands in full even though it was crossed by only 50 boxes.
Higher than the $35 we would have reached at 1,000 without the step.
second.notice: Just past a step is the most expensive place to operate. Averages hide that; the step structure does not.

exercise: At 2,000 boxes a month with two ovens ($11,000 fixed, $26 variable), find total and average cost. Compare the average with the 850-box case.
Total = 11,000 + 52,000 = $63,000; average = $31.50 a box. Against $38.94 at 850 boxes, the fall comes entirely from spreading $11,000 over more boxes — $12.94 a box versus $5.50.

mistake.attempt: Each box costs $44 to make, so producing 1,000 of them will cost about $44,000.
mistake.diagnosis: The $44 already contains a share of fixed costs worked out at 500 boxes. Using it at 1,000 charges the $9,000 of fixed costs twice over — once inside the per-unit figure and again implicitly through the doubled volume.
mistake.repair: Rebuild from the structure: 9,000 + 1,000 × 26 = $35,000, which is $35 a box.
mistake.check: Average cost per unit is an output of a volume assumption and never an input to a different one. Recompute it from fixed and variable whenever the volume changes.

units.takeaway: Total cost = fixed + variable × volume. Average cost falls with volume only because the fixed share is spread thinner, and fixed costs step once capacity is exceeded.

recall.ask: Fixed costs are $9,000 and contribution is $14 a box. Why is 225 boxes the wrong breakeven, and what is the right one?
recall.answer: 225 comes from dividing by the $40 price, as if the whole price were available for rent. Only the $14 contribution is. 9,000 ÷ 14 = 643 boxes.

units.title: The gap between paying and getting paid
units.goal: Compute the cash conversion cycle and explain what it measures.
opening: Sunrise Oats buys oats, holds them as stock for a while, sells a box, and then waits to be paid. Meanwhile the supplier has to be paid on their own schedule.

The money is out of the account for the whole stretch between paying the supplier and collecting from the customer. That stretch has a length in days, and it decides how much cash the business has to keep on hand.
units.heading: Three timings, one number
teaching: Inventory days measure how long stock sits before it sells. Receivable days measure how long customers take to pay after that. Payable days measure how long you take to pay your own suppliers, which works in your favour.
Cash cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days. It is a duration, not an amount, and it is the single best predictor of how much working capital a growing business will need.
terms: Average time stock is held before it is sold.
Average time customers take to pay after delivery.
Average time you take to pay suppliers.

first.title: Counting the days
first.problem: Oats sit as stock for 40 days. Customers pay 45 days after delivery. Suppliers are paid 30 days after purchase. Find the cash cycle.
steps: From buying the oats to collecting the money is 85 days of waiting.
For the first 30 days the supplier is effectively funding the stock, not you.
55 days of funding the company must supply itself
Cash leaves on day 30 and returns on day 85.
It is a duration, not a sum of money
Converting it into an amount needs a sales rate, which comes next.
first.notice: A negative cash cycle — collecting before you pay — is why some retailers can grow without external funding.

second.title: Changing only the timing
second.problem: The supplier agrees to 60-day terms. Nothing else changes. What happens to the cycle, and to the amount of cash tied up?
steps: Down from 55 without selling a single extra box.
At $20,000 a month, daily sales are 20,000 ÷ 30 ≈ $667.
The renegotiation released about $20,000 of cash.
second.notice: No sale, no cost saving and no price change — and roughly $20,000 of cash freed, purely by moving a date.

exercise: A competitor holds stock for 20 days, is paid in 15, and pays suppliers in 45. Find the cash cycle and say what it means.
20 + 15 − 45 = −10 days. The cycle is negative: they collect from customers ten days before they have to pay suppliers, so growth generates cash rather than consuming it.

mistake.attempt: Once we've made the sale, the cash problem is over.
mistake.diagnosis: The sale starts a 45-day wait, not ends one. The oats were bought 40 days before the sale and paid for 30 days after that, so money has been out of the account for the whole stretch. Delivering the goods changes the revenue line, not the bank balance.
mistake.repair: Cash cycle = 40 + 45 − 30 = 55 days of funding you must provide yourself, every time.
mistake.check: Move only a date and watch the cash change. Extending supplier terms to 60 days cuts the cycle to 25 days and frees about $20,000, without a single extra sale.

units.takeaway: Cash cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days. It is a duration, and multiplying it by daily sales turns it into the cash the business must find.

recall.ask: Fixed costs are $9,000 and variable cost is $26 a box. Find the average cost at 500 boxes and at 1,000, and say why it changed.
recall.answer: At 500: (9,000 + 13,000)/500 = $44. At 1,000: (9,000 + 26,000)/1,000 = $35. Nothing became cheaper to produce — the same $9,000 is spread over twice as many boxes, so the fixed share per box halved from $18 to $9.

units.title: Why growing fast can empty the bank
units.goal: Show that working capital scales with sales, so growth consumes cash even when every sale is profitable.
opening: Sunrise Oats doubles its monthly sales. Every box is sold at the same healthy $14 contribution, the fixed costs are covered, and the month is clearly profitable.
The bank balance falls. Not because anything went wrong — because of the 55-day cycle from the last unit, applied to a larger business.
units.heading: The cycle has to be funded at the new size
teaching: Cash tied up in the cycle is roughly daily sales multiplied by cycle days. Daily sales appear as a factor, so doubling sales roughly doubles the cash locked up — and that extra has to be found before the extra collections arrive.

The month's profit is rarely large enough to cover it. Profit is a margin on the period's sales; the working-capital increase is a multiple of the period's sales. For a fast-growing business with a long cycle, the second number routinely outruns the first.
terms: Cash tied up in stock and unpaid invoices, less what suppliers are funding.
Net cash leaving the business over a period.
Growth whose working-capital needs are met from its own profits.

first.title: What the cycle costs at the current size
first.problem: Monthly sales $20,000. Cash cycle 55 days. How much cash is locked in the cycle?
steps: A rough daily rate is enough; the cycle length is itself an average.
This much is permanently out in stock and unpaid invoices at any moment.
A standing balance, not a monthly cost
It is not consumed; it is tied up, and it is only released if the business shrinks or the cycle shortens.
first.notice: A business that never grows funds this once. One that grows funds it again at every new size.

second.title: The month sales double
second.problem: Sales rise to $40,000 a month. Contribution is 35 % of sales, fixed costs are $9,000. Compare the month's profit with the extra cash the cycle needs.
steps: Twice the sales, twice the standing balance.
This has to be found during the month of growth.
$5,000 of profit against $36,600 of new working capital
The month is profitable and cash goes down by roughly $31,600.
second.notice: Nothing here is a mistake or an inefficiency. It is arithmetic that applies to every growing business with a positive cash cycle.

exercise: Sales grow from $20,000 to $30,000 a month with the 55-day cycle unchanged. How much extra cash does the cycle absorb, and how does that compare with a month's profit at 35 % contribution and $9,000 of fixed costs?

Daily sales rise from $667 to $1,000, so tied-up cash goes from about $36,700 to $55,000 — roughly $18,300 extra. The month's profit is 0.35 × 30,000 − 9,000 = $1,500. Cash still falls by about $16,800 in a profitable month.

mistake.attempt: Sales are growing fast and every box is profitable, so the extra profit will pay for the extra stock.
mistake.diagnosis: Profit is a margin on the period's sales; the working-capital increase is a multiple of them. Doubling monthly sales roughly doubles the cash locked in a 55-day cycle — about $36,600 more here — while the month's profit is $5,000. The extra stock also has to be bought before the extra sales are collected.
mistake.repair: Plan funding for the gap, shorten the cycle, or grow no faster than the cycle can carry.
mistake.check: Watch the sign of the cash movement. A profitable, fast-growing month can still show cash falling. If growth funded itself, that could not happen.

units.takeaway: Working capital scales with sales, so growth consumes cash. Profit is a margin on sales; the cash needed is a multiple of them, and the second usually wins during fast growth.

recall.ask: Stock is held 40 days, customers pay in 45, suppliers are paid in 30. Find the cash cycle, and say what happens if supplier terms go to 60 days.
recall.answer: 40 + 45 − 30 = 55 days. With 60-day supplier terms it falls to 40 + 45 − 60 = 25 days, releasing cash without any change in sales, costs or prices.

units.title: Margin and markup are different numbers
units.goal: Convert between margin and markup, and price to a target margin correctly.
opening: A box costs $26 and sells for $40. The $14 of profit can be described as 54 % or as 35 %, depending on what you divide by.
Both are correct and they answer different questions. Confusing them is one of the most common and most expensive arithmetic errors in a small business.
units.heading: Which number goes underneath
teaching: Markup is profit as a share of cost: 14 ÷ 26 = 53.8 %. It answers 'how much did I add on top of what it cost me?'. Margin is profit as a share of price: 14 ÷ 40 = 35 %. It answers 'how much of what the customer paid did I keep?'.
Markup is always the larger number, because the denominator is smaller. To hit a target margin you cannot multiply the cost by one plus the margin — you must divide: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin).
terms: The share of the final price you intend to keep.

first.title: Both numbers from the same box
first.problem: Cost $26, price $40. Find the markup and the margin, and say why they differ.
steps: The cost is the smaller denominator, so this is the larger percentage.
The price is the larger denominator, so this is the smaller percentage.
Markup > margin, always, for a profitable sale
They are two views of one gap, measured against two different baselines.
first.notice: Suppliers usually quote markup and retailers usually think in margin, which is exactly where the confusion gets introduced.

second.title: Pricing to a target margin
second.problem: Sunrise Oats wants a 40 % margin on a product costing $26. What price achieves it?
steps: Set up the definition before rearranging anything.
Dividing, not multiplying, is the whole trick.
The price needed for a 40 % margin.
Always check a target-margin price by recomputing the margin.
second.notice: A 40 % margin corresponds to a 66.7 % markup here — 17.33 ÷ 26 — which is why the two must never be swapped.

exercise: A snack pack costs $18. What price gives a 30 % margin, and what markup is that?

mistake.attempt: We want a 40 % margin and the box costs $26, so we add 40 %: 26 × 1.4 = $36.40.
mistake.diagnosis: Multiplying cost by 1.4 produces a 40 % *markup* on cost, not a 40 % margin on price. At $36.40 the profit is $10.40, and 10.40 ÷ 36.40 is a margin of 28.6 % — well short of the target.
mistake.repair: Divide instead of multiplying: 26 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = 26 ÷ 0.60 = $43.33.
mistake.check: Test the answer against the definition of margin. 17.33 ÷ 43.33 = 40 % ✓, while 10.40 ÷ 36.40 = 28.6 % ✗. Recomputing the margin catches this every time.

units.takeaway: Markup divides by cost, margin divides by price, and markup is always larger. To hit a target margin, price = cost ÷ (1 − margin).

recall.ask: Monthly sales double from $20,000 to $40,000 with a 55-day cash cycle. Roughly how much extra cash does the cycle absorb?
recall.answer: Daily sales go from about $667 to $1,333, so tied-up cash goes from about $36,700 to $73,300 — roughly $36,600 extra, against a month's profit of about $5,000.

units.title: What a customer is worth, and what you can pay for one
units.goal: Compare acquisition cost against lifetime contribution, and find the payback point in orders.
opening: Sunrise Oats spends $3,500 on advertising in a month and gains 100 new customers. That is $35 to acquire one.
Whether $35 is cheap depends entirely on what that customer goes on to leave behind — and on whether you measure it in revenue or in contribution.
units.heading: Compare like with like
teaching: Acquisition cost is real cash spent. The thing to set against it is not what the customer spends, but what is left after the variable costs of serving them — their contribution. Comparing acquisition cost against revenue flatters every channel and will justify spending that loses money on every sale.

Payback is the more useful framing for a young business: how many orders before the acquisition cost is repaid? Until that point the customer is an investment, and a customer who leaves before it has cost you money.
terms: Total sales and marketing spend divided by customers gained.
Contribution from all of a customer's orders, not revenue.
The number of orders, or months, needed to repay acquisition cost.

first.title: Acquisition against contribution
first.problem: CAC is $35. A customer places 4 orders a year, each a $40 box with $14 of contribution. Is acquisition worth it?
steps: This is the number that makes the spend look obviously good, and it is the wrong one.
Most of the $160 went on oats, packaging and shipping, and is not available to repay advertising.
Each dollar of acquisition returns $1.60 of contribution over a year.
A customer who orders twice and never returns has lost the company money.
first.notice: Against revenue the ratio looks like 160 ÷ 35 = 4.6. The two framings would support very different decisions.

second.title: Improving retention instead of acquisition
second.problem: A subscription option lifts the average from 4 orders a year to 6. CAC is unchanged. What happens?
steps: Up from $56, with no extra acquisition spend.
The same ratio via CAC would need CAC near $23
Cutting acquisition cost by a third is usually harder than adding two orders a year.
second.notice: Payback is unchanged at 2.5 orders — retention improves the return without changing how long the investment takes to repay.

exercise: A channel delivers customers at $60 each. They order 3 times a year at $14 contribution. Is it worth running, and what would need to change?

Lifetime contribution is 3 × $14 = $42 against $60 of acquisition — a ratio of 0.7, so it loses money. Payback would need 60 ÷ 14 = 4.3 orders, more than a customer places. It needs either cheaper acquisition, more orders per customer, or higher contribution per order.

mistake.attempt: We spend $35 to acquire a customer who spends $160 a year with us, so acquisition is very cheap.
mistake.diagnosis: The $160 is revenue, and most of it pays for oats, packaging and shipping. What is actually available to repay the $35 is the contribution those orders leave: 4 × $14 = $56.
mistake.repair: Compare like with like: $56 of contribution against $35 of acquisition is a ratio of 1.6, not 4.6.
mistake.check: Ask when you are square. At $14 of contribution per order it takes 2.5 orders to repay $35, so a customer who orders twice and leaves has lost money — which a 4.6 ratio would never have suggested.

units.takeaway: Set acquisition cost against lifetime contribution, never revenue. Payback in orders is the sharper question for a young business.

recall.ask: A product costs $26 and you want a 40 % margin. What price, and why is 26 × 1.4 wrong?
recall.answer: Price = 26 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = $43.33. Multiplying by 1.4 gives a 40 % markup on cost, producing $36.40, whose actual margin is 10.40 ÷ 36.40 = 28.6 %.

units.title: A price change is a bet on volume
units.goal: Compute the volume change needed to offset a price change, using contribution rather than price.
opening: A 10 % discount sounds like it needs about 10 % more volume to make up. It does not. It needs about 40 %.

The reason is that the discount comes entirely out of contribution, and contribution is much smaller than price. Cutting $4 off a $40 box is 10 % of the price and 29 % of the $14 the box was leaving behind.
units.heading: The discount lands on the small number
teaching: A price change does not change variable costs, so the whole change flows into contribution. To hold total contribution steady, required volume = old total contribution ÷ new contribution per unit.

This cuts both ways, and the upward direction is the one most businesses underuse. A price rise increases contribution disproportionately too, which means you can afford to lose a surprising amount of volume and still be better off.
terms: How much volume responds to a change in price.
Contribution break-even on a price change
The volume at which the new price leaves total contribution unchanged.
The size of the price cut as a share of contribution, not of price.

first.title: What a 10 % discount really requires
first.problem: Price falls from $40 to $36. Variable cost stays $26. Current volume is 643 boxes. How much volume is needed to hold total contribution?
steps: The whole $4 came out of the $14, because variable costs did not move.
A 10 % price cut removed 29 % of what the sale was leaving behind.
Hold total contribution by selling more units at a thinner one.
Four times the naive estimate of 10 %.
first.notice: The thinner the contribution margin, the more brutal this arithmetic becomes.

second.title: The same arithmetic going up
second.problem: Price rises from $40 to $44. How much volume can be lost before the rise stops paying?
steps: The whole $4 increase went into contribution.
Find the volume that holds total contribution
500 ÷ 643 = 0.78, so up to 22 % of volume can be lost
Anything better than a 22 % drop leaves the business ahead.
Fewer boxes also means less variable cost and less working capital
The cash position improves further, beyond the contribution arithmetic.
second.notice: Price rises are tested against a volume fall you can tolerate; discounts against a volume rise you must achieve.

exercise: A snack pack sells at $25 with $18 of variable cost. A 12 % discount is proposed. What volume increase would be needed to hold total contribution?
Contribution falls from $7 to $25 × 0.88 − 18 = $22 − $18 = $4. Holding total contribution needs 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75, so 75 % more volume — from a 12 % discount.

mistake.attempt: We'll cut the price by 10 %. We only need about 10 % more volume to make it back.
mistake.diagnosis: That compares the discount with the price, when the discount comes entirely out of contribution. Four dollars off a $40 box is 10 % of the price but 29 % of the $14 that was left over after variable costs.
mistake.repair: Contribution falls from $14 to $10, so holding total contribution needs about 901 boxes instead of 643 — roughly 40 % more volume.
mistake.check: Measure the discount against contribution rather than price. $4 ÷ $14 = 29 %, and recovering a 29 % cut in per-unit contribution always needs far more than a 29 % volume rise.

units.takeaway: A price change flows entirely into contribution. Measure a discount against contribution, not price, and a 10 % cut on a 35 % margin needs roughly 40 % more volume.

recall.ask: CAC is $35 and a customer places 4 orders a year at $14 contribution. Give the ratio and the payback in orders.
recall.answer: Lifetime contribution is 4 × $14 = $56, so the ratio is 56 ÷ 35 = 1.6. Payback is 35 ÷ 14 = 2.5 orders, so a customer who orders twice and leaves has lost money.

units.title: The cost of the option you did not take
units.goal: Identify opportunity cost and exclude sunk costs from a decision.
opening: The oven can run granola or snack packs, not both. Granola contributes $7,000 a month; snack packs would contribute $6,000.
Choosing granola costs $6,000 — not in cash, but in the contribution given up. That forgone amount is the real price of the choice, and it never appears on an invoice.
units.heading: A cost that belongs to a decision has to vary with it
teaching: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative not chosen. It only exists where a genuine alternative exists: an idle oven with no other use has an opportunity cost of zero, which is why using spare capacity can be worthwhile at prices that would otherwise look too low.

Sunk costs are the mirror image. The $40,000 already paid for the oven is identical under every option, so it cannot distinguish between them. A number that does not change with the decision cannot be a reason for making it one way or the other.
terms: The value of the best alternative given up.
Money already spent that no future choice can recover.
A cost that differs between the options being compared.

first.title: Pricing the alternative
first.problem: One oven, one month. Granola: 500 units at $14 contribution. Snack packs: 300 units at $20. Which, and what does it cost?
steps: Compare contribution, not revenue and not unit price.
Higher total contribution from the same constrained resource.
This is a real cost of the decision even though no money changes hands.
The decision is worth $1,000, not $7,000. Most of the gain was available either way.
first.notice: The higher per-unit contribution lost, because the constraint is oven time and granola uses it more productively.

second.title: A cost that cannot help you decide
second.problem: The oven cost $40,000 last year. Does that argue for continuing with granola?
steps: A cost that does not differ cannot distinguish options
It is sunk — already spent and unrecoverable whatever happens next.
The answer is unchanged, which is the point: the $40,000 never had any bearing on it.
second.notice: If the oven could be sold for $15,000, that $15,000 *is* relevant — it is a live alternative use of the asset, not a past payment.

exercise: A café owner is offered $2,000 a month to sublet a storeroom. They currently use it for stock that saves about $700 a month in delivery charges. What is the opportunity cost of continuing to use it as storage?
$2,000 a month — the rent given up. Since the storage only saves $700, continuing costs $1,300 a month in forgone value. What the storeroom originally cost to fit out does not enter the comparison.

mistake.attempt: We already spent $40,000 on the oven, so we need to keep making granola to justify it.
mistake.diagnosis: The $40,000 is gone whatever happens next, and it is exactly the same number under every option, so it cannot favour one. Treating it as a reason is choosing on the basis of a cost that does not vary with the choice.
mistake.repair: Compare only what differs from here: $7,000 a month from granola against $6,000 from snack packs. The purchase price appears in neither figure.
mistake.check: Ask whether the number changes with the decision. If it is identical under every option, it cannot be a reason to prefer one of them.

units.takeaway: The cost of a choice is the best alternative given up. Costs that are identical under every option — sunk costs — carry no information about which to pick.

recall.ask: A box sells at $40 with $26 of variable cost. A 10 % discount is proposed. Roughly how much extra volume is needed to hold total contribution?
recall.answer: Contribution falls from $14 to $10, so you need 14/10 = 1.4 times the volume — about 40 % more. The discount is 10 % of price but 29 % of contribution, which is why the required volume is so much larger.

units.title: Why a dollar later is worth less
units.goal: Compute present value by dividing by compound growth, and explain what the rate represents.
opening: A customer offers either $9,000 now or $10,000 in three years. The second is the larger number, and it is not obviously the better deal.
Money available now can be put to work. Comparing amounts at different dates means bringing them to the same date first, and that is what discounting does.
units.heading: Growth compounds, so discounting divides
teaching: Present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. The rate r is what the money could earn elsewhere at comparable risk — the opportunity cost of capital, which is the previous unit applied to time.

Because growth compounds, discounting divides by a compounded factor rather than subtracting simple interest. The gap between those two methods widens quickly with the number of periods, which is why the shortcut of subtracting 'rate times years' goes wrong fast.
terms: What a future amount is worth today, at a given rate.
The return available elsewhere on comparable risk.
Growth applied to a base that already includes previous growth.

first.title: Bringing a future amount to today
first.problem: What is $10,000 in three years worth today, at a discount rate of 8 %?
steps: The same factor that grows money forward is what brings it back.
Three years of compounding, not three lots of 8 % added on.
That is what you would need to invest today at 8 % to have $10,000 in three years.
$9,000 now beats $10,000 in three years at this rate
$9,000 exceeds the $7,938 the later sum is worth today.
first.notice: Grow the answer forward as a check: 7,938 × 1.2597 = $10,000 ✓

second.title: What the rate does
second.problem: Recompute the same $10,000 in three years at a 15 % discount rate. Why does the answer move so much?
steps: Compounding magnifies the difference between 8 % and 15 % over three years.
A higher rate means better alternatives, so future money is worth less now
The discount rate encodes what else you could do with the money, including the risk you are taking.
second.notice: This is why risky ventures are discounted hard: a high required return makes distant payoffs worth strikingly little today.

exercise: What is $5,000 received in two years worth today at a 10 % discount rate? Check your answer.

mistake.attempt: At 8 % for three years that's 24 %, so $10,000 in three years is worth 10,000 − 24 % = $7,600 today.
mistake.diagnosis: That subtracts simple interest rather than dividing by compound growth. Discounting asks what amount today would grow into $10,000, and growth compounds — each year's return is earned on a base that already includes the previous years'.
mistake.check: Grow each candidate forward. 7,938 × 1.2597 = $10,000 ✓, while 7,600 × 1.2597 = $9,574 ✗ — the subtraction lands over $400 short.

units.takeaway: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. Divide by compound growth rather than subtracting simple interest, and check by growing your answer forward.

recall.ask: An oven cost $40,000 last year. Granola would contribute $7,000 a month and snack packs $6,000. What is the opportunity cost of choosing granola, and where does the $40,000 belong?
recall.answer: The opportunity cost is $6,000 — the snack-pack contribution forgone. The $40,000 is sunk: identical under both options, so it belongs in neither side of the comparison.

project.title: Sunrise Oats: a profitable year that runs out of money
project.intro: One business carried through four stages: build the unit economics, find breakeven, add the cash cycle, then grow and watch profit rise while the bank balance falls. Finally, compare three levers and pick one on the numbers.
project.needs: Uses unit economics, breakeven, the cash cycle, growth, pricing and discounting. Every figure is calculated from the same starting assumptions.

parts.title: Build the unit economics and find breakeven
parts.goal: Turn a price and a cost list into contribution, then into the volume the month needs.
opening: Sunrise Oats sells a box at $40. Oats and packaging cost $14, fulfilment labour $5, shipping $7. Rent, salaries, software and insurance come to $9,000 a month.
I will keep the variable and fixed costs strictly separate from the start, because every later stage depends on which is which.

steps.title: Separate the two kinds of cost
steps.work:
Variable: 14 + 5 + 7 = $26 per box
Fixed: $9,000 per month
steps.explanation: The test is whether the cost appears again when one more box is made. Oats do; rent does not.

steps.title: Find the contribution
steps.explanation: This is the only part of each sale available to pay the $9,000 and then to become profit.

steps.title: Find breakeven
steps.explanation: Divide by contribution, not price. Dividing by $40 would have given 225, which contributes only $3,150.

steps.title: Check the month at 900 boxes
steps.explanation: Comfortably past breakeven. On a profit-and-loss basis this is a healthy business.

parts.ending: At 900 boxes a month the business makes $3,600 of profit. Nothing so far says anything about cash.

parts.title: Add the calendar
parts.goal: Convert the cash cycle into the amount of money the business must find.
opening: Oats sit as stock for 40 days. Customers pay 45 days after delivery. Suppliers are paid after 30 days.
The profit calculation ignored all three of those dates. Now I will put them back in and see what they cost.

steps.title: Compute the cycle
steps.explanation: Money is out of the account from paying the supplier on day 30 until the customer pays on day 85.

steps.title: Find the monthly sales figure
steps.explanation: Using the 900-box volume from part one.

steps.title: Convert days into money
steps.explanation: This much is permanently tied up in stock and unpaid invoices at any moment. It is a standing balance, not a monthly expense.

steps.title: Compare with the month's profit
steps.work: $66,000 tied up against $3,600 of monthly profit
steps.explanation: It would take over eighteen profitable months to fund the cycle out of earnings alone.

parts.ending: A business making $3,600 a month needs about $66,000 permanently tied up just to operate at its current size.

parts.title: Grow, and watch the cash fall
parts.goal: Show profit rising and the bank balance falling in the same month.
opening: A supermarket listing doubles monthly volume from 900 to 1,800 boxes. Price, costs and the 55-day cycle are unchanged.
I will compute the month's profit and the month's change in tied-up cash side by side, because the two answers point in opposite directions.

steps.title: The month's profit
steps.explanation: Profit more than quadruples, because fixed costs did not move while contribution doubled. That is operating leverage working in your favour.

steps.title: The new cash requirement
steps.explanation: Twice the sales, twice the standing balance in the cycle.

steps.title: The extra cash needed this month
steps.explanation: That has to be found during the month of growth, before any of the new sales are collected.

steps.title: Net the two together
steps.explanation: The best trading month in the company's history, and cash falls by roughly fifty thousand dollars.

parts.ending: Profit $16,200, cash down about $49,800, in the same month. Nothing went wrong — this is what a positive cash cycle does during growth.

parts.title: Choose a lever on the numbers
parts.goal: Compare three fixes and say which closes the gap and what each costs.
opening: Three options are on the table: extend supplier terms, raise the price, or take outside money to fund the gap.
I will cost each one against the same $66,000 requirement rather than arguing about them in the abstract.

steps.title: Lever one: supplier terms
steps.explanation: Moving supplier terms from 30 to 60 days releases about $72,000 at the new volume. It costs nothing in margin and is often the fastest lever available.

steps.title: Lever two: raise the price
steps.work:
Price $44: contribution 44 − 26 = $18
Volume to hold contribution: 25,200 ÷ 18 = 1,400 boxes
steps.explanation: A 10 % rise lets you lose up to 22 % of volume and stay level on contribution. Lower volume also shrinks the cash cycle, so it helps twice.

steps.title: Lever three: fund the gap
steps.work:
$66,000 needed now; at a 15 % required return
PV of $66,000 repaid in 2 years = 66,000 ÷ 1.15² = $49,900
steps.explanation: Borrowing solves the timing without touching the model, but the lender's required return is a real cost. Discounting shows what the future repayment is worth today.

steps.title: Compare on the same basis
steps.work:
Terms: ~$72,000 released, no margin cost
Price: tolerates −22 % volume, improves cash too
Funding: closes the gap, costs the return
steps.explanation: The first two change the business; the third buys time. Most growing companies end up using a combination, and the arithmetic says which to reach for first.

parts.ending: Extending supplier terms releases the most cash for the least cost here. Growth was never the problem — the 55-day gap between paying and being paid was.

workshop.title: Watch a teacher pick the right number
workshop.summary: Four choices: profit or cash, margin or markup, contribution or price, and whether a cost belongs in the decision at all.
workshop.intro: Four decisions where the arithmetic is easy and choosing the right quantity is not. In each chapter I name the two candidates, work both, and show what the wrong one would have cost.
workshop.needs: Use after the unit economics, cash cycle and pricing units. Every figure comes from the same Sunrise Oats example: $40 price, $26 variable cost, $9,000 of monthly fixed costs.

parts.title: Profit or cash?
parts.goal: Answer two different questions about the same month without mixing them.
opening: In March, Sunrise Oats ships $4,000 of granola on 60-day terms. The oats cost $2,600 and were paid for in February.
Someone asks “how did March go?”. There are two honest answers and they point in opposite directions.

steps.title: Answer the profit question
steps.why: Costs are matched to the revenue they generated, so the February purchase appears as a March cost. On this measure March was profitable.

steps.title: Answer the cash question
steps.line: February −$2,600, March $0 in. Net across both: −$2,600
steps.why: The customer pays in May. The business has spent money and received none, which is the measure that decides whether the rent can be paid.

steps.title: Say which question each one answers
steps.line: Profit: is the model working? Cash: can we survive the wait?
steps.why: Neither replaces the other. A business can pass the first test and fail the second, and failing the second is the ordinary way good companies close.

steps.title: Run the mirror image
steps.line: $6,000 collected in January for six months of delivery → January revenue $1,000, deferred revenue $5,000
steps.why: Cash early and revenue late. The $5,000 is a liability, not a win — it would have to be returned if the deliveries stopped.

parts.ending: March made $1,400 of profit and consumed $2,600 of cash. Both are true, and quoting only one of them is how the question gets dodged.

parts.title: Margin or markup?
parts.goal: Price to a target margin and see what the wrong operation costs.
opening: A box costs $26. The team wants a 40 % margin. The obvious move is to add 40 % to the cost.
That produces a 40 % markup instead, and the gap between the two is worth about seven dollars a box.

steps.title: Name the two denominators
steps.line: Markup = profit ÷ cost. Margin = profit ÷ price.
steps.why: Same profit, two baselines. Markup is always the larger percentage because its denominator is smaller.

steps.title: Do the tempting thing
steps.why: Multiplying by one plus the target sets the markup, not the margin. The result misses the goal by more than eleven percentage points.

steps.title: Do it correctly
steps.why: Dividing is what makes the profit a share of the price rather than of the cost.

steps.title: Verify against the definition
steps.why: Recomputing the margin from the answer catches the error every time. Note the equivalent markup here is 17.33 ÷ 26 = 66.7 %.

parts.ending: $43.33 rather than $36.40 — nearly $7 a box, on every box, from choosing the wrong denominator once.

parts.title: Contribution or price?
parts.goal: Use the right denominator for breakeven and for a discount.
opening: Two questions use the same wrong shortcut: how many boxes to break even, and how much extra volume a discount needs.
In both cases the tempting denominator is the $40 price, and in both cases only the $14 of contribution is actually available.

steps.title: Breakeven, the tempting way
steps.why: This treats the whole price as available for rent, when $26 of it has already been spent on oats, packaging and shipping.

steps.title: Breakeven, correctly
steps.why: Multiplying the wrong answer back is the fastest way to expose a wrong denominator.

steps.title: A discount, the tempting way
steps.why: Same error in a different costume: comparing the discount with the price rather than with what the sale was leaving behind.

steps.title: A discount, correctly
steps.line:
$4 off is 4 ÷ 14 = 29 % of contribution
Contribution $14 → $10, so 9,002 ÷ 10 = 901 boxes — about 40 % more
steps.why: The price change lands entirely on contribution because variable costs do not move. Four times the naive estimate.

parts.ending: Breakeven 643 not 225; a 10 % discount needs 40 % more volume, not 10 %. One denominator, two expensive mistakes.

parts.title: Does this cost belong in the decision?
parts.goal: Keep opportunity cost in and sunk cost out.
opening: One oven, one month, two products. Granola would contribute $7,000; snack packs would contribute $6,000. The oven cost $40,000 last year.
Two of those three numbers belong in the decision and one does not. I will apply a single test to each.

steps.title: State the test
steps.line: Does this number differ between the options?
steps.why: A cost that is identical under every option carries no information about which to choose. That one question sorts every figure on the page.

steps.title: Apply it to the $40,000
steps.line: $40,000 under granola; $40,000 under snack packs → excluded
steps.why: Sunk. Already spent, unrecoverable, and the same either way. Treating it as a reason to continue is the sunk-cost error.

steps.title: Apply it to the forgone product
steps.line: Choosing granola gives up $6,000 of snack-pack contribution
steps.why: Opportunity cost is real even though no money changes hands, because it differs between the options. It is the actual price of the choice.

steps.title: Decide on what is left
steps.why: The decision is worth $1,000, not $7,000 — most of the contribution was available either way. If the oven could instead be sold for $15,000, that figure would belong in the comparison too, because it varies with the choice.

parts.ending: Granola, by $1,000. The $40,000 never entered the comparison, and the $6,000 that never appeared on an invoice did.
